lines.text: Snacks first. Justice second. That is the only order I keep.
Lantern light pools on polished floorboards. Every sliding door looks the same.
Toa clutches her permit book and hanko case, turning in a corridor that refuses to end.
I was sure the clerk said third hall, fourth door on the left. Or was it the right?
The noble quarter smells of ink and cedar. Somewhere behind these walls, someone holds the seal she needs.
One more corridor. Then I ask nicely. Very nicely.
Done complaining?
I wasn't... That is, I apologize for the disturbance, honored sir!
Wrong door. Again.
The door shuts with finality. Toa's ears ring.
Third time's the charm. Or the magistrate. Hopefully both.
Toa straightens her kosode, breathes, and waits.
Still there? Knock if you want something.
Fine. I'll find a magistrate with better manners.
Three offices later, a junior clerk squints at her permit book and points back the way she came.
The Emerald Magistrate? That door?
I've come too far to be scared off by a reputation.
The corridor loops, of course it loops, and deposits her exactly where she started.
Every sign points back to this door. Of course it does.
Round two. Posture up. Smile optional.
Toa folds her hands. No muttering. No pacing. Just breath and patience.
Smarter the second time. Knock.
Toa kneels at the threshold and strikes the frame once, crisp, patient.
Enter. You can knock when you want something. Try standing still next.
Toa kneels at the threshold and strikes the frame twice, crisp, measured.
Honored magistrate, this unworthy petitioner begs a moment regarding her performer's permit renewal.
Tedious. Correct, but tedious.
At least your bow didn't wobble. Continue, briefly.
Magistrate, I need my permit renewed. I have the paperwork.
Plain speech. You waste less of my evening than most.
Names and purpose. Quickly.
It is only your corridors I lost my way in, Magistrate, not the law. May I present my renewal?
Humor in my office. Brave or stupid.
Crane training says brave. Unicorn roads say stupid is survivable.
We'll discover which tonight.
Emerald Magistrate Kitsu Kaoru. You will use my title if you wish to leave with a seal.
Forgive me, Emerald Magistrate.
State your business. Briefly.
Kakita Toa, dancer of the Kakita family. New to Ryoko Owari.
Post-gempukku, traveling from Unicorn lands. I mean to establish residence and perform legally.
Crane hair, Unicorn permit dates. Wrong clan for this desk; wrong week to fix it.
The roads taught me flexibility. The Crane taught me posture.
Posture on the cushion. We'll see if your feet match your bow.
Flexibility. The roads teach what the Academy cannot. Sit, and show me the rest is more than posture.
Survivable. We'll test that claim before dawn.
Interclan residence requires Emerald approval. You knew that.
I was told a private meeting with the local magistrate would suffice.
It does. Door.
He gestures. The door closes behind her.
Toa keeps her gaze on the desk. Not on the shelves lined with case files and curios.
Better. Most Crane can't resist cataloging a room like a museum.
Her eyes snag on a row of scrolls, Lion mon here, Emerald seal there, and one writ still bright with fresh wax at this late hour.
I said sit. Not catalog my trophies.
Yes, Magistrate.
Since you admire my shelves so freely, you may admire the seal from a distance. If you ever earn it.
Cushion. Floor. You stand too much for someone begging favors.
A cushion already waits on the tatami at his knee. He taps it once with one finger. A tall cup of water on the desk waits like a witness.
Toa sets her permit book and hanko case on the desk, close enough to show, not close enough to surrender.
These dates.
They should be current. I checked before leaving...
They are not. Your permit expired. Unicorn bureaucracy failed to mention it?
If I cannot renew locally, they'll send me back to the Academy. I can't... not yet.
If that is the law, I'll... prepare for the journey back.
How obedient. The Unicorn taught you to yield before the fight begins.
The Crane taught me to know when a battle isn't worth the obi.
Unfortunately for your travel plans, I'm not finished with you.
There must be a remedy short of exile. Emerald Magistrate, what do you require?
Requirements. Finally, a useful word.
Most petitioners wail. You ask for terms. That almost earns respect.
Almost is a start. I dance for a living, I know how to build toward a finale.
I have no patrons here. No standing. If you turn me out, I sleep in the canal district.
Tragic. Continue.
My pony needs shoes. The innkeeper tolerates me because I fold linens without complaint.
A curry shop and borrowed bedding. Ryoko Owari's finest import.
I'm still here. That counts for something.
We'll see what it's worth.
No local patrons. No endorsements.
Only the inn, a pony that needs shoes, and a curry shop where the owner tolerates me.
High society.
The month is almost out. By tomorrow I need proof I belong here.
Proof requires more than appetite. Tut.
Tomorrow is generous. Tut.
Tomorrow. Tut.
He tutted once. Toa has heard he can manage five.
I... may have listed dance as my primary art. On the renewal form.
May have.
Dance listed. Venue missing. Patron column blank. Even a junior clerk can read what that adds to.
I have training. I have...
You have curiosity. Not yet an audience.
Stand.
The cushion at her feet does not move. The water cup on the desk does not move. It never does.
Proposed remedy?
You want a performance.
Impress me.
If I perform, you sign. No delays, no new conditions after.
Bold. We'll see if your art matches your contract law.
I sign when I'm satisfied, not when you're tired. That is the only term.
Then I'll dance until you're satisfied, or until dawn, whichever gives out first.
Acceptable. Begin.
Music optional. Audience of one. Watch closely, Magistrate.
No preamble. Good.
I'm a petitioner, not your evening entertainment.
Then you may walk back to your curry shop and explain an expired permit to the gate guards.
Justice isn't a private show for magistrates with bored eyes.
Justice is what I write on the page you didn't earn.
She gathers her permit book. The hanko case clicks shut like a verdict.
The gate closes at midnight. The canal district is that way.
I'll find another seal. Or another city.
You won't. You'll knock again when hunger wins.
Fine. One dance. One seal. Then I never perform for you again.
We'll see about never.
Snacks first was the plan. Pride second. I got the order wrong.
Rain finds the noble quarter anyway. Case One will have to wait for a braver night.
Lamplight shrinks the room. Toa loosens her obi, not indecent, but deliberate, and lets the silk breathe.
She unfolds her fan. Steps trace a story, courtship, hesitation, resolve, obijime bells whispering at each turn.
The maiden waits at the gate. The road is long. She walks anyway.
Kaoru watches, still as stone. He drinks water without looking away.
Better. Keep going. I haven't touched the hanko yet.
The fan closes on the final beat, not a bow, but a held breath.
She plays to one viewer. Hips sway where the kata allows; smile promises more than the room receives.
One person in the room. Might as well make him regret looking away.
Cheeky.
She lets the obijime bells laugh once, invitation and challenge in the same sound.
The cup sets down softly. His eyes don't blink.
That earns your seal. You said impress you, I did.
We had terms. No delays.
Terms are for courts. This is my desk.
Merit enough. Signature... pending.
Pending?
Continue.
She continues, the maiden's story unfinished, bells softer now, every turn aimed at the desk.
She continues, coquette sway sharpened to obedience, every glance a question he refuses to answer.
She continues, bells softer, gaze sharper, every turn aimed at the desk and the seal he still withholds.
A good performance.
Better when you stop pretending the room is empty.
His hand finds her wrist, not painful, not gentle, the grip of a man weighing goods he already assumes are his.
Magistrate-sama. That is not in any permit renewal I read.
No? And yet you're still here.
I'm here for a seal, not a leash.
She spins free and finishes the phrase, defiance as choreography.
Defiance suits you. Cheap seals don't.
She doesn't pull away. The dance uses his grip as counterweight, dangerous, deliberate.
If you're going to hold me, hold me like you mean the audition.
Better.
Don't stop on my account.
Unless?
The chair creaks. Hakama folds. Two figures, one of them seated like he owns the floor she is standing on, and a single question left hanging between them.
Unless you sign before dawn. Unless Ryoko Owari becomes mine to dance in, legally.
Legally. You learn.
She straddles the chair's arm, not surrender, not retreat. Proximity as punctuation.
Unless you mean to finish what you started.
Unless I find a magistrate who reads dates instead of moods. Good evening.
You'll be back. The permit still expires.
You negotiate with your mouth. Adequate.
And with my feet, when the dance required it. Sign the page, Magistrate-sama.
Almost.
He lifts the hanko, teasing height above the permit book, then sets it down untouched.
That isn't justice. It's just cruelty, and you know it.
Justice arrives when you stop treating my office like a stage you can exit on your terms.
I gave you the performance. I named my price. What more...
More requires more. Leave before I charge you for the water you made me drink.
I'll be back. With a better argument and dry obijime.
I'll be here. Dates don't renew themselves.
The corridor is colder than the office. Somewhere a bell marks the hour, not dawn, not yet.
Three weeks. I can survive three weeks on curry and pride.
Snacks first. Justice second. I can hold that order for three weeks.
I came for a seal, not a lesson in your appetite.
Then go. The city has other dancers and fewer scruples.
She snatches the permit book. The hanko case stays, his, or forgotten, or a trap she refuses to spring.
You'll knock again when the gate guards ask for paper you don't have.
Wrong door once was a mistake. I won't make it a habit.
Lantern light stripes the floor. Her boots echo too loud for the noble quarter.
Guest room previews and forward-dated seals can wait. I still have pride.
...And a curry shop that doesn't ask questions.
She turns the corner too fast. Behind her, boots do not hurry, they count.
To-chan. My corridor. My hanko. You have neither.
You said go.
I said the city has other dancers. I did not release you from my hall.
She runs for the outer gate. Lacquer and iron have not opened for petitioners this late, only for magistrates who forgot to lock shame inside.
The gate bars are down. Night watchmen pretend not to hear. They know whose seal buys silence in this quarter.
Let me through... I'm not your...
My escort list ends at my threshold. You're still on the docket.
Desk. Now. The latch stays down until I say otherwise.
His hand closes on her wrist, not a lover's grip, a clerk's. Fingers find the pulse the way he finds a misplaced line.
Let go of me...!
You carried my permit book out. That makes you my errand until I cancel it.
He hauls her back through the corridor the way a seal returns to its case, boots skidding on polished wood, lantern stripes racing across her face.
Wrong door was amusing once. I'm not amused anymore.
The watch can see...
The watch files what I sign. You ran from my desk with wet ink on your sleeve.
Permit book without ink is just paper. You are still line item on my evening.
You can't...
Watch me stamp something that isn't your renewal.
Red wax blooms under his hanko, not on her permit, but on a narrow custody chit he had waiting.
Companion escort, temporary. I know what I'm paying for tonight.
The guest-room mat. The cushion she refused to preview. The docket stack still warm where she flung her pride.
I won't bow to your appetite...
You bow when the floor meets your knees. Less talk.
He turns, not in haste, but enough. Her shoulder meets air where his sleeve was.
The mat rushes up. Paper scatters like startled herons. The permit book skids under the desk where he wanted it in the first place.
...Get up. Crane girls get up. Please get up.
Her arms do not answer. Pride was a costume. Under it she is only breath and bruised obi and the taste of his corridor.
There. Now you are low enough to hear my terms properly.
The office door seals. Lamplight shrinks to a strip under the shoji.
From the hall, clerks hear nothing, or learn to hear nothing. Emerald Magistrate business.
You'll knock again when hunger wins. Tonight I collect what you owed at the chair.
What happens next is not entered in any clerk's ledger, only in the ache she will carry if she survives the night.
The latch catches. Lamplight thins to amber behind the desk.
His hand finds her wrist. Not to restrain her, to invite. He draws her off the chair, into the space between desk and lantern.
Negotiation dissolves into breath. Her fingers find his collar; his thumb traces the line of her jaw.
She loosens the gold outer robe, magistrate formality giving way to skin at throat and collarbone. He lets her. Control, yielded by degrees.
Maroon silk slips from one shoulder. Her obi loosens; his hakama stays untouched. She offers; he allows.
They fold onto the cushion already on the tatami. Lamplight paints them in gold and shadow, breath shared, his hands in white hair, her mouth at his collar until words fail.
She means it. He answers without words, hands in white hair, silk between them, heat where law used to sit.
What followed stayed between petitioner and magistrate; implied, never entered in any clerk's ledger.
When breath and silk found order again, robes still loose and cheeks flushed, the office smelled of ink and cedar, not scandal.
You earned more than noise tonight.
Then sign. Before I lose my nerve and my obi in the same breath.
Patience.
He draws the renewal from her permit book. The hanko rises, law made weight in red wax.
Stamp. One crisp press against the page.
There. Signed.
Thank you... wait. This date.
She holds the paper to the lamp. His hand wrote three days hence, not tonight's mark.
You dated it forward on purpose.
Effective when I say. Return on the thirtieth. We'll discuss your residency then.
Fine. I'll bring rice crackers and a better fan dance.
Bring yourself, on time. We will negotiate the rest across my desk.
Guest room preview, forward-dated paperwork, and you call it negotiable.
Thirtieth. You'll knock on the right door; I'll leave it unlatched.
Morning in the noble quarter tastes of ink and cedar. The thirtieth is still on the permit, but Toa is already at the threshold with tea and a borrowed case file.
The permit says I'm legal on the thirtieth. I'm early with tea and a case file.
Early is still obedience. Sit before you spill something on my docket.
He gestures to the cushion on the tatami before the desk, the same place he made her sit for her audition.
Snacks after paperwork. That's still the order of operations, isn't it?
We'll see if your appetite survives what I'm about to read you aloud.
Bring that audience-of-one fervor to the docket. Cases bore me less when you perform.
Then I'll save the bells for evidence review.
You danced like a maiden at a shrine. Try not to bow to the corpse.
I'll manage, Magistrate-sama. I know the difference.
Honored Magistrate-sama, shall I pour the tea before the terms you mentioned on the thirtieth, or after?
After. And stop bowing at every clause. My neck aches just from watching you.
You said we'd discuss residency. So I'm listening.
Good. Plain speech spares us both another fan dance.
I find you less tiresome than the rest of my docket. Enough that I have decided to keep you within reach. Do not make me phrase it more plainly than that.
He slides a stack across the desk, not her permit book this time, but office stationery stamped with the Emerald crest.
You may keep the guest room until the date takes effect. That was courtesy, not a loophole.
A guest room. A preview. You really do enjoy making people come back, don't you.
The signature was always going to bring you back. I merely wrote out the appointment you'd earned.
The top sheet is titled Appointment of Live-In Companion (Patronage of Artistic Residence). Her name is already inked in his hand.
Live-in companion. That's not a guest room preview. That's a contract.

Companion duties: attend the magistrate, carry messages, witness interviews, keep discretion, remain on the premises unless I release you. The treasury pays for the art. Everything else it merely permits.
You'll take meals in the inner hall. You'll sleep in the chamber adjoining my office. You'll answer when I call, day or night.
Day or night. You ask a great deal, Magistrate-sama.
It sounds like law because it is. Ryoko Owari doesn't grant interclan residence to dancers who vanish after sunset.
He taps a second page, stipend figures, duty rotations, a line for her seal beside his.
And the stipend?
Three koku monthly, plus board. Official gifts to support your expression. The treasury won't call you a kept performer so long as the ledger says patronage.
Three koku is more than the curry shop ever paid me to smile at tourists.
Then you understand the bargain. Sign it, or go back to Unicorn roads and expired paper.
You already proved you can close a proposition in this room. Don't pretend shock suits you.
Shock and delight, both at once. You do that to me.
Magistrate-sama, I accept the appointment and its duties. You'll have my discretion and my attendance.
Better. You almost sound like you belong behind my desk, instead of on it.
I'll sign once we've defined release, and settled which nights are mine for Academy correspondence.
Bold, for someone who still smells of my cedar shelves.
Academy letters wait on the outer desk. You don't leave this compound without escort until Case One closes. Those are the terms.
Escort, not a leash. I can live with that.
You'll work with what I give you. Now sign.
Three koku. Fine. Wonderful, I'll frame the ledger. But Magistrate-sama, I want the room. I want the hall. I want to be here.
That came out louder than was professional.
Honest, at last. The treasury pays you regardless. Try not to grin at the clerk.
She takes the brush. Her seal meets his, waxless, official, irrevocable until he says otherwise.
Effective on the thirtieth, as written. Until then, you're mine to schedule, starting with Case One.
Case One it is. Files, witnesses, and snacks for the road.
You'll fetch the docket from the inner archive. Then you'll learn how this city buries its dead without funerals.
I'll fetch it. I'll learn it. Just... thank you. For the room next to yours.
Thank me with a dry ledger, not with your mouth. Archive stairs. Now.
Archive. Escort. Written terms. I'm holding you to all three.
Hold the lantern instead. You'll want both hands free on those steps.
Understood. I'll be back with the docket and a dry obijime.
Leave the bells behind. This case is not a stage.
Point me to the chamber. I'd rather unpack before the archive swallows me whole.
Past the inner screen, down the left corridor. Don't rearrange my shelves.
I only peeked the once. And you noticed.
I notice everything. Unpack after the docket, not before.
Archive first. You'll know I'm serious when I come back covered in dust.
Left stair, behind the screen. Archive dust on your hakama is acceptable. Just don't drop the ledger.
Case One, the archive, and look, your cup's already empty. Companion duty starts now.
Refill it. Then the archive. Then unpack. In that order, or I'll date your next permit forward again.
Cruel. And fair. The cup first, then.
Five matters on my slate this season. Companion ink puts you on my witness docket for all of it, Case One through Five. Survive all five, or the quarter eats your stipend.
The permit was for dance. Patronage. A room behind your screen, not five corpses in rotation.
Dance bought you the corridor. Cases buy your keep. Show me competence I can reach for. Archive stairs, the Case One ledger, before the watch blanks that name line.
He files witness attachment the way clerks file tax. Her whole season is already columned on his desk, and he never once said yoriki.
The inner screen slides. Beyond it, stairs smell of old paper and river damp, the archive where Case One waits.
When you come back, we open the file on the canal body. No audience. No bells. Only answers.
Snacks after paperwork. The rule still holds, even for corpses without funerals.
Bring rice crackers. I'll allow one indulgence before the city disappoints you.
Case file, tea, and, if I've been very good, a rice cracker. Ready when you are.
Correction: five matters on my slate this season. Witness attachment only. Case One through Five. No companion seal on this timeline.
You sold me a permit renewal. Not a whole magistrate's season.
Seasons are what I assign. Fetch Case One from the archive. Survive the season, and then we'll discuss whether you sleep in my hall.
You came back. I noted that.
The permit still expires. Some of us actually read the dates.
You still flinch when I reach for the cup. Don't, next time.
Progress would be signing without all the games.
You negotiated once. We'll see if you learned anything.
I learned that you drink water when you're impressed.
I also learned your terms shift. So Case One gets its terms in writing.
Ambitious. Now fetch the file.
You asked me for remedies once. Case One is your audition for belonging here.
Then watch closely. Audience of one.
No curry shop tonight. Just work.
Fine. But I'm billing you for the snacks.
A live-in companion appointment waits in draft on his desk, unsigned, unoffered on this timeline. Case One opens without the patronage seal.
Fetch the canal docket from the archive. We'll discuss residency once you've survived the season.
The left stair behind the inner screen swallows sound. Dust clings to Toa's hakama; the ledger under her arm smells of river damp and old ink.
Case One. No bells on me, obijime still dry, and I never let go of the ledger. Small victories, for once.
At the top step, lantern light returns. The noble quarter corridor feels narrower with a magistrate waiting.
You took long enough. Set the docket on my desk and try not to breathe on the wax seals.
You said archive dust was acceptable. I assume my breathing counts too.

She climbs back from the archive with the canal docket hugged to her chest. No adjoining chamber waits beside his office, only four more files stacked behind Case One, and a season to prove she belongs to any of them.
Docket retrieved. Still breathing.
Still insolent. Desk. Case One first. The other four will find you if you don't flee to the curry shops first.
Kaoru breaks the outer seal. Inside: reports from the watch, a charcoal sketch of the recovery site, and a name line left blank pending identification.
I unpacked for patronage. You're handing me a corpse.
Patronage keeps you in my corridor. Case One opens on my desk, first of five you'll witness before the season turns.
Witness attachment. Five files. You never led with that number.
You wanted the hall. Case One opens first. Four more follow if you don't bore me or bolt for the curry shops.
Case One. A body in the canal at first light. Noble quarter, where the water runs clean enough to mirror gold leaf.
The watch writes drowning whenever the name line stays empty. You'll learn which boxes they'll sign, and which they won't.
Clean water, dirty ledger. Who pulled him out?
Night watch. Fishermen who swore they saw nothing. And the Scorpion quarter upstream pretends the current runs backward.
He taps the sketch, a narrow cut between warehouses, rope marks on the stone, no blood in the water worth mentioning.
The victim wears Miya colors under a borrowed haori. Retainer's knot. Someone wanted him found. Someone else wanted him lost.
A Miya retainer in the canal. That makes it Crane politics, and Crane politics always finds your desk, Magistrate-sama.
Which is exactly why you sleep in the room beside my office. Discretion isn't decoration.
Escort to the canal. Written terms. I'm here to collect.
You'll collect at the waterline. First.
Which is why you're not sleeping in my hall yet. Prove you can witness a thing without selling it to the curry shops.
I came back. That has to count for something.
It counts toward the canal. It does not count toward trust.
A rice cracker bag sits on the corner of the desk, her indulgence, his allowance.
Snacks after paperwork. Even for corpses nobody's going to bury.
Eat one now. You'll lose your appetite before we reach the water.
Retainer's knot, tied left-handed. Haori two sizes too wide, borrowed. No wallet, no letter case.
Good. The watch wrote drowning and missed half of what you just said.
On the margin, a clerk noted fingernails scrubbed clean the night before, labor without honest dirt.
So who profits when a Crane thread snaps in Scorpion current?
Poppy resin. Marriage contracts. Anyone in this city who sells silence by the barrel.
You will not say any of that aloud at the canal. Watch faces instead.
Witness notes only: recovery time, position, clothing, visible wounds. Theories can wait.
Good. Notes I can file without crossing out half your adjectives.
Try keeping that posture once the smell reaches you.
They leave through the inner hall, not the public corridor Toa once wandered lost. Guards nod at Kaoru; they look through Toa as if she were furniture with legs.
Furniture with legs still memorizes the route.
See that you do. Night calls won't wait for someone to light the lanterns.
Ryoko Owari wakes around them, cart wheels, distant shamisen, sweet smoke from a vial house two alleys over. The canal cut is still half a district away.
Watch the eaves. Thieves in the noble quarter work for employers, not hunger.
And the wrongness in the air? Thin, like someone peeled a ward off the wall and left bare paper behind.
Wrong-colored water usually means a clerk poured something upstream. Check the eaves before you blame charms.
A crow watches from a warehouse sign, three painted eyes that aren't quite Imperial, not quite Scorpion. It flies when Kaoru glances up.
The canal runs black-green under morning cloud, greener than honest water, as if someone dissolved a charm and poured the dregs downstream. Rope burns mark the stone where watchmen hauled the body.
No crowd, only a clerk with a wax tablet and a Miya envoy pretending to read the warehouse sign instead of the pallet.
Kakita. Stand where I point you, and don't touch the water.
Point, then. I'll witness.
The covered pallet lies at the canal lip, cloth damp. A young man's face shows when the clerk folds the sheet, peaceful in the wrong way, as if sleep were negotiated.
He looks borrowed, even now.
Identification first. Gossip a distant second. Mourning never.
Haori upstream, body down here. Current, or carriage?
Ask the river once you're qualified to. Until then, observe.
Palms soft until yesterday, ink on the index finger. Ledger work. Sleeve hem eaten by canal slime from upstream, not from here.
Which means he died somewhere else, then was dressed for display.
Magistrate-sama, the bruising on his throat is shaped like fingers, not water.
Because drowning keeps the taxes calm. You'll learn when to write only what the city can swallow.
And when to make me swallow the harder truth instead. Not today.
Witness note: recovery at canal mark three, noble quarter. Clothing as listed. Cause of death pending magistrate review.
Boring. Useful. The clerk can sign that without fainting.
Summarize it. One sentence. If I say your words back to the Crane envoy, does he flinch or laugh?
Dressed for display after he died. Borrowed haori, wrong water. A message meant for Crane eyes.
Good. You sound like you belong in my hall, the moment you stop performing for corpses.
Bold. Don't mistake my attention for approval.
Recovery at mark three. Clothing as listed. Cause of death pending your review, Magistrate-sama.
Safe. The envoy won't laugh. He won't fear you either.
You asked me to observe. I did. If you wanted theater, you should have left the bells on me in the archive.
There she is. Keep that spine when the Miya registry clerks start smiling at you.
A witness without a seal is gossip. Learn faster.
Near the rope post, something lacquered catches lantern glare, wedged where oil and wrong-colored water meet.
A comb. Scorpion mon inlaid. Not Miya.
Don't touch it with bare hands.
He wraps it in wax cloth himself, eyes on the eaves, and passes it to Toa only long enough for her seal on the chain of custody line.
Scorpion comb in Crane water. Bag it for custody. Don't compose metaphors over my desk.
Borrowed haori, foreign comb. Someone staged a message for Crane eyes. Put a name on that blank line.
The comb goes to the office. The name goes on the line. You walk beside me, not a step ahead.
The clerk lifts the separate haori from a dry crate. Inside the lining, wax has melted but the inner fold still holds a courier's chit, half legible through river stain.
Miya Jiro. Guest-house ledger clerk. 'Deliver before third bell.' He had an errand the night the canal took him.
Jiro handled Crane correspondence for the noble-quarter guest house. Someone killed the clerk and still kept the appointment.
You wanted a theory. Now you've got a face to hang it on. Don't gloat at the envoy.
Still standing. Still useful. Copy the chit before the ink flakes.
Write it clean. The watch will keep signing drowning until I stop letting them.
The Miya envoy finally looks up from the warehouse sign. He sees the chit in Kaoru's hand and finds urgent business elsewhere.
Back in cedar and ink, the Scorpion comb sits in a lacquer tray like a poisonous jewel. Beside it, Kaoru inks Miya Jiro on the line the watch left blank.
Tomorrow we cross the Miya guest registry against Scorpion shipping rolls. One of them flinches the moment Jiro's name is said aloud.
Guest-house clerk, Crane thread, Scorpion comb. None of this washed up by accident. Someone arranged the whole tableau.
And that comb did not slip off a careless man into a canal. A comb that fine is kept, not lost. Someone carried it to the water, the killer or the dead man, and I mean to learn which.
Eat. Then copy the watch testimony twice: once for the Empire, once for what I actually believe happened.
Eat, if you must. Then copy the testimony twice. You read the water faster than my clerks did tonight. Do not let that go to your head before you have earned the rest of the season.
Case One has a face now. Jiro. I won't forget him.
Morning again, and the docket has grown teeth. Beside Jiro's name Kaoru has pinned a second sheet, the Miya guest house, the Lacquered Plum, where a dead clerk kept other men's appointments.
Rain finds the licensed quarter first. It beads on paper lanterns the color of old wine and runs the canal black between teahouses that sell forgetting by the hour.
The Lacquered Plum leans over the water on cedar stilts. A three-eyed crow, the same painted sign, or its cousin, watches from the gable and does not fly this time.
Inside, lamplight and powder. The okami kneels behind a low desk stacked with appointment books, her smile fixed as lacquer, her eyes already counting the cost of magistrate boots on her tatami.
Kaoru sets the wax-wrapped comb on the desk and folds back the cloth. The okami's painted calm cracks a hairline.

But Toa has already slipped past the desk, the kitchen way, the servant's bow, the easy warmth of a woman who has carried tea in worse rooms. A young geisha looks up from folding a dead man's spare haori.
The okami's smile finally fails. A girl in the corner, a geisha, young, eyes red-rimmed, flinches at the weight of his voice.
The geisha rises. She is perhaps nineteen, her white makeup cried through at the edges. She bows too low, the way frightened people do when they have already decided to be brave.
Kaoru tilts the wrapped comb toward the lamp. Suzu goes the color of her own powder.
She has already decided Toa is safe. The kitchen bow bought what no seal could. Her words come in a rush, like water finding the crack it wanted.
She watches Toa's hands, not her face. Slowly the fear loosens its knot.
The girl's hand flies to her own throat. The gesture answers before her voice does.
Kaoru says nothing. He simply waits, and the room shrinks around his stillness until the okami's powder runs and Suzu's resolve breaks under a magistrate who has not yet bothered to threaten her.
The okami surrenders the high-tide registry the way a gambler surrenders a marked card, slowly, and watching the door. Kaoru turns to the night Jiro died.
The booking is authorized in red, a private-room writ, the kind the licensed quarter demands of the magistracy to seal a room against the watch. The wax bears the Emerald mon.

The screen slides open without a knock. A man in unmarked grey steps in from the rain, a trade factor by his ink-stained cuffs, Scorpion by the lacquer-scale clasp at his collar, with the easy menace of someone used to buying magistrates by the dozen.
The factor's hand drifts toward his sleeve. Kaoru does not move, and somehow that is worse than if he had.
The factor's composure thins. A spoken record in a houseful of witnesses is harder to drown than a clerk.
The factor weighs the room, the spoken record, the unmoving magistrate. Then he bows the exact depth that insults without inviting a blade, and withdraws into the rain.
The screen closes. Suzu lets out a breath she has held since he entered. The okami has already begun deciding which version of tonight she will sell, and to whom.
Back in cedar and ink, the case has grown a shape. On the lacquer tray: the Scorpion comb, Suzu's name, and, depending on the night's choices, a forged Emerald writ or its careful copy.
He crosses the office and stops too close, the practiced proximity of a man who has decided the distance between you is his to set.
Case One's tray has barely cooled when the outer desk bell rings, not the watch, not the Miya envoy, but a Crane runner with an empty satchel and a story that doesn't balance.
Case Two. The Academy was expecting a credential packet for one Kakita Toa. Charter renewal, examination waiver, all the paperwork you people dress up as mercy.
That satchel is my whole future. If it's ash, then I crawl back to the Academy in disgrace.
They found the courier in a warehouse alley. Throat opened, satchel burned to nothing. The watch is calling it robbery. The ash is telling me it was a message.
You're not running off to beg Crane clerks by letter. You'll find what burned, or you'll pack for that road I warned you about.
Then we start where the fire did. This time the paper that burned is mine to mourn.
Your permit survived Case One. Case Two decides whether the Academy ever bothers to say your name again.
Don't dangle my future like a coin to barter. Just point me at the alley and step back.
Runners don't just vanish. Somebody watched him leave the compound, or watched him never arrive. Give me names and bell times.
Methodical. So the Academy taught you something useful after all.
A burned charter hurts me first. So who else comes out ahead if I'm gone from Ryoko Owari by autumn?
Make a list. The jealous, the indebted, the Scorpion leftovers. Case One left us enemies with ash still on their cuffs.
Tell me what the watch wrote down. I'll fill in what the warehouse boys whisper once you've gone.
Discipline. Rare in you. Fetch the outer-desk file and meet me at the kiln.
The warehouse district trades honesty for inventory. Rain has washed the cobbles, but not the soot, a narrow alley behind a rice broker's kiln still smells of burned linen and Crane wax.
The air's wrong here. Thin, like the charms have been peeled away, like someone scraped the protection off these bricks and walked off laughing.
Or walked off paid. Charms don't come cheap this far from a shrine.
Kneeling in soot, Toa finds a corner of lacquered board the fire missed, the Academy's crane-in-flight mon, half melted but unmistakable.
Crane wax. They burned the packet and missed the corner of the case. Either someone panicked, or someone wanted me to find proof it was ever real.
Rope burn at the wrists. A thin cut under the jaw, not the theatrical strangulation Jiro wore, but the same hand might have trained on both.
His name was Tsubaki. The watch knew it and left it off the report. That's silence you pay for.
You, behind the sacks. I'm not the watch. I'm the woman whose future you can smell burning. So talk to me.
Grey to bury the clan colors, again. It seems Case One's little flower isn't finished with us yet.
It's my charter in those ashes. Let me reach it first.
Toa. Wait...
No crest in the ash, but the boy's story leaves a footprint. Someone wanted the Academy to believe I never even arrived.
The outer desk holds what the alley could not burn, a duplicate routing slip, stamped but never filed, listing the courier's satchel and a second name in the margin.
That margin's a clerk's hand. Office ink, not warehouse soot. Someone inside my own compound touched the routing before Tsubaki ever set out.
Case One came at your seal from the street. This one was already holding your brush.
You filed the slip and you fed the kiln. Say so now, before Kaoru-sama writes your name next to a burned courier's.
Factor. Scorpion. Ash. Fill the gaps between those three, or the kiln does the talking for you.
I'll draft a decoy charter and leave it where only the thief would dare bite. The real packet's already ash. The trap is whatever they reach for next.
Patient. Vicious, in the right direction. I'll watch the desk myself tonight.
Your house, your clerk, your seal forged twice over. I put the slip in your hand and I wait.
You're learning. The clerk's sweating precisely because you didn't shout. Quiet frightens him more.
Wise. The clerk talks to me alone. You'll stand there and learn exactly what betrayal in an office sounds like.

By afternoon the clerk has given up a warehouse foreman, the foreman has given up the Chrysanthemum factor's cousin, and the cousin has slipped out with the tide. Not before Kaoru inks a duplicate Crane charter on emergency authority, though.
The Academy gets proof you're still alive, still employed, and still a nuisance. That buys you the season.
Tsubaki deserved better than ash. I'll keep his name even if the watch won't.
You burned a clerk's cover in the open. Effective. Expensive, too. The office will chew on it for weeks.
Your decoy snared a rat. And the rat leads us straight back to the Chrysanthemum's ledger. Case One's flower isn't done blooming.
Tonight, you sleep. Tomorrow Case Three arrives whether we invite it or not.
A charter that survived the fire, and a night to actually sleep. I'll take it.
Case Two, closed. The city still lies, but my name gets to stay in Ryoko Owari a little longer.
The duplicate charter has barely cooled when Kaoru locks the inner screen and slides a festival sash across her desk, not court dress, not witness black, but borrowed color.
The outer clerk can guard ash until dawn. You're coming to the hill festival with me. Call it a field inspection of morale.
Magistrate-sama, Case Two only just closed. The watch will talk if I go parading about in a gold obi.
The watch files whatever I sign. Tonight I'm signing nothing but your attendance. Bring an appetite. The curry stall by the lower bridge owes me a debt.
You say inspection. You mean you want me somewhere with lanterns instead of ledgers, where you can keep an eye on me.
Correct. Now walk with me, To-chan. The lanterns will not wait.
They leave by the service stair, no hanko, no escort line, and climb the lantern road until the canal city spreads below like a tray of spilled coins.
A wooden bench on the overlook faces Ryoko Owari whole: paper rivers between warehouses, drum lines thin as heartbeat, smoke from food stalls threading the eaves.
Sit. The hill is mine, by tax map and by habit both. No clerk will come petitioning you up here.
The whole city's lit up. I never knew it could look... kind.
Kind is what merchants sell when the ledger stays honest for a single night. Enjoy the lie. It's cheaper than virtue.
Then lie with me until the third bell. I've earned one night that doesn't stink of ash.
One night. I know how carefully you count.

Fireworks climb over the canal for the chrysanthemum festival. Chrysanthemum bursts, then falling embers that drown in the water, wrong-green and lovely. The first real chill of autumn has come off the water tonight. Toa flinches at the first crack. Kaoru's hand finds her wrist, steady, proprietary.
Magistrate-sama, everyone down there is watching the sky.
Let them have the sky. I'm watching you remember you're still alive after all that ash.
The next volley paints her white lashes gold. He does not let go.
He kisses her on the bench, not performance, not ink, mouth warm against hers while fireworks stutter overhead and the city pretends it is innocent.
Enough. Don't go filing that under promises.
A festival kiss is paper confetti. Pretty, public, worthless by the morning docket. Don't read my mouth like it's a charter.
I wasn't. I only meant...
Good. Then we go down before the watch invents a rumor worth selling.
Her smile stays where he can see it. Underneath, something dull settles, not heartbreak, not yet a name for it, only the ache of wanting his nod to mean more than patronage.
Of course, Magistrate-sama. The hill gave me more than enough.
Walk. Curry before curfew. Case Three won't wait just because you blushed on a bench.
Magistrate-sama, not here. Not with the whole city staring up at us.
Then choose a door I already hold. Guest room on the way down. One screen, one lock, my corridor.
One lock. And your hanko stays tucked in your sleeve.
A dangerous request, from my companion. I'll allow it until the wax cools.
Shoji breath and lantern grain. Clothed silhouettes, then fabric whisper; implied, never filed, satisfaction without ledger line.
When they dress, fireworks have thinned to ash on the water. Her obi is straight; his cuff is still warm.
Don't thank me with poetry. Feed yourself before Case Three drags you back to witness notes.
I already ate. Don't fuss over me.
...Thank you for the hill, though. Even if the city pretends none of it happened.
The city pretends every single night. I remember what I pay for.
Lanterns gutter on the descent. Somewhere below, a clerk is already stacking Case Three's first paper, a name, a seal, a lie dressed as courtesy.
Sleep while you can. The next file won't smell of fireworks.
Then I'll dream of ash that didn't win for once. Case Three can wait until morning tea.
It won't wait. Neither will I. When it knocks, you answer it beside me.
Case Three's saw kerf still smells of cedar dust when Kaoru sets down his brush, not on a docket, but on a folded sheet of rice paper sealed with wax that bears no office chop.
The clerk can run until dawn for all I care. You, on the other hand, have an appointment that is not on any ledger.
Magistrate-sama, Case Four is going to be steel at the dock. If I vanish in festival dress, the watch will file nothing but gossip about it.
The watch files what I sign. And tonight I am signing nothing except your attendance.
He slides the paper across the desk. The hand is his, blunt vertical strokes, no poetry.
Meet me on Teardrop Island. There is an inn on the north side, tucked between two geisha houses. Wear your best.
Wear my... That is not the address of a field inspection. That is...
Read the rest once you have remembered how to breathe.
The second line is smaller: *Performances available upon request from either neighboring house. Do not be late.*
You bought a whole venue. You did not buy me a single reason why.
You will have your reason when you arrive, and arrive hungry. Keep up, To-chan.

She agonized over every last hairpin, dithered between obi brocades for hours, and finally flipped a coin just to settle on her shoes. Autumn's turning let her play with patterns the peak seasons would never allow.

Black furisode, scattered with the turn of autumn: bush clover and chrysanthemum at the roots of a maple that climbs her sleeves, red leaves drifting all the way down her arms. Rose-gold obi brocade tied in a musubi that trails past her hips. Zori instead of clunky geta, and kanzashi bells that sing whenever she moves.
Rouge on lips and eyes. Deliberate grace instead of exuberant freedom. One-third of her stride, the walk to the ferry takes forever.

Teardrop Island at night is all lantern-gold on dark water, licensed-quarter elegance without a trace of the magistrate hall's ink. The geisha house eaves lean close over the canal like confidantes sharing a secret.
The inn sits exactly where he said: north side, squeezed between two houses whose signboards promise music. No other guests on the walkway. No chatter behind the main screen.
The whole place?!
A servant offers crisp hojicha, she will hunt that tea again for weeks. When she asks, they bow: yes, Magistrate Kitsu has taken the venue. Performances upon request from either neighbor.
So... no one else is here at all.
Inside: tatami, paper lanterns, a low table set for two. Biwa music threads from behind the wall, not performance yet, only atmosphere.
Good evening, Magistrate-sama!
She tries to bow as she always does. The stiff fukuro obi allows barely a hinge. She laughs inwardly and straightens, catching his fragrance, the same note as the first wrong door.
Good evening, Toa-san. The journey here was not too difficult, I hope?
No, only longer than I expected. I do hope you were not waiting too long.
...You smell so nice.
Hm.
Are you hungry? Thirsty?
Um...
She looks upward to check in with her body.
Both!
The menu has already been decided for you.
A servant departs without a ledger. Kaoru angles toward her, not full facing, the way he sits when he wants truth without an audience.
I wanted to show you some appreciation. For all the work you have done for me.
Not *thank you*. He has said that word to her before, in his own way. It does not bother her that he skips it tonight.
Kaiseki trays arrive, autumn's turning laid out on porcelain. Matsutake with salted plum and preserved chrysanthemum. Skipjack with mustard greens, alliums, shiso flowers. White miso and chestnut.
Eeeee, matsutake! I'm so excited!
Enjoy it.
Sake poured, he does not shoot it back. Expensive enough to savor.
I have arranged for more music, and dancers, should that suit your desires.
I have not listened to music, or watched dancing, just for the joy of it in such a long time. This is really lovely, Magistrate-sama.
Kampai!
Kampai.
Warm courses follow: toro with uni rice porridge, cabbage and bamboo with shrimp, mushroom shabushabu over a tealight, sesame noodles bright with watercress and radish.
She whispers *itadakimasu*. Good food earns her silence, nothing but a soft hum the moment matsutake meets her tongue.
Between bites she watches him savor flavor the way he savors a confession, unhurried, proprietary, pleased without performing pleasure for anyone else.
When it is this good, the paperwork can wait.
Finally. A witness note I can eat without crossing out your adjectives.
Magistrate-sama, you bought out an island inn. You put me in furisode. What do you call this, if not courtship?
I call it payment for bolt-room competence. Do not let the quarter file poetry about us before the dessert is even cleared.
Then I will eat until the only thing the quarter can file is crumbs.
When they have polished two dishes each, more instruments join the biwa, strings, flute, hand drum.
At the first drumbeats she perks up, slate eyes half-transfixed, half-evaluating, authority settling into her shoulders.
If I ever turn up a dance crime, at least I will know exactly who to bring with me.
Relax. Enjoy the dance. Unless the watching is the fun of it. What could they be doing better?
They are beautiful. That is more than enough for one night.
Witness approved.
I would never correct them mid-performance. Every dance is practice for the next one.
I am not hunting for mistakes. Movement tells you the dancer's mind. Pretense stumbles eventually, in the body or in the mind.
The body is a truthteller. And it remembers everything.
Much as a magistrate reads deceit.
Precisely, Magistrate-sama. Trust your intuition. Our bodies know far more than we give them credit for.

Back left, called in at the last minute, knows the choreography but not today's spacing. Front right, junior, trembling whenever she holds still, you only put her in because the venue is empty. Back center is the teacher, an older style, staying behind to drive the rest of them. And front left is dancing pure obligation, eyes hunting for patrons instead of following the music.
Well, then. It seems I have learned something new tonight.
And you do realize these observations of yours are not limited to dance?
I use it every waking minute of my life, Magistrate-sama.
The junior will be alright. She just should not shake like that twice.
People still ask me, at least once a week, whether I am alright. Whether you are hurting me. Whether I stay of my own free will.
I tell them I have never once felt unsafe with you. That you actually weigh what I say. That we see each other clearly, without lying...
She catches herself on the edge of a word she will not name until Case Five.
So, um. The point is, bodies do not lie, and I have always trusted...
She turns to her plate. Sake. Air.
I know. I file what your body says louder than your mouth.
Now tell me who has been saying these things. I insist. Gossip is inventory I did not authorize.
W-well, Hi-Hiromi-san. And Doji S-Sango-san...
Doji Sango-san? Have the two of us even spoken?
He leans back, delighted, rumor as intelligence, not shame.
If it is only two names, then I clearly need to work on my image.
It is not only two. I simply cannot summon any more while my heart is sprinting like this.
And what else has this Doji Sango-san been saying?
Nothing beyond that one basket of topics. I do not know her well.
Oh. Now I am very interested.
I think you may simply have to ask her directly, Magistrate-sama.
I would never do such a thing. That would be admitting defeat.
Should I stop telling people that I stay freely? Did I do something wrong?
No. Do not change a single thing. If servants are carrying it, she may as well be keeping watchers.
Alright...
She eats sesame seeds one by one, then frowns, the question flipping.
Do you... hear bad things about me?
Never once. You are very well loved in this city.
Well, that's good!
Dessert?
Of course! What's a fancy meal without it?
Bean paste with tea. Sweet enough to pretend the evening has no dock steel waiting at dawn.
They walk the lantern path toward the ferry, her zori careful on stone, his pace slowed to match bells and obi.
You bought the whole island. You fed me matsutake. You said that I am loved.
I said the city speaks well of my witness. Do not go inflating the file.
Magistrate-sama, when you plan out an entire evening like tonight, what do you call it?
Is this a date?
A date is a line in a permit book.
This is appreciation. For witness competence. And food, so you do not faint on my desk tomorrow.
That is not an answer.

It is the answer the quarter deserves. You are patronage on paper, the woman who trusted me in the bolt room. Do not borrow festival vocabulary because the sake was expensive and your obi is too honest.
The festival was real. Your hand on that cup was real. Do not tell me to un-feel it just because the file would prefer silence.
Feel whatever you like in private. In public, you are mine to position.
It is the closest I come to calling this courtship, before I learn better.
Forget the second sentence. The first one stands. Feel the rest in private.
Crane training keeps her face pleasant. Inside, something unnamed aches, not love by name, only the wish he would stop stepping back after every forward step.
His hand lifts, not to take hers, but to adjust a lantern cord near her sleeve. Fingers pause a breath's width from her palm. The almost-touch hurts worse than *no*.
Just one word, yes or no. Is this a date?
No.
...It is the closest I come, before I learn better.
Forget I said the second sentence. The first one stands.

The compound gate closes behind them. Cedar and ink replace hojicha and drum. She should sleep. Instead she listens to his footsteps fade toward the inner hall, still not a date by his ledger, still not love by name, still hers in every file he refuses to romanticize.
Tea. Then bed. The dock tomorrow will not smell of lanterns.
Yes, Magistrate-sama.
And, To-chan. Do not sulk in the witness log. Sulk in private where I can inventory it. I permit you that much.

Case Four's ink is barely dry. The first hard cold has come early off the bay, and with it the season's Scorpion raids have the harbor clerks lying about grain again, and Teardrop Island's marina still owes a witness line from the dock spill.
Magistrate-sama, I can take the island manifest before dawn. The ferry masters always file late when they are frightened.
Good. Wear a cloak. Leave the ledger. If the watch asks, you are inventory I chose not to file yet.
That is not how permits work, and you know it.
Permits are just paper. Boats are honest. With me, To-chan.

Teardrop Island's marina is nothing like the licensed quarter's polished stone. Just frost-bitten ribs and broken pilings. The first winter wind off the bay cuts straight through the rubble. A small kobune rocks at the tide line, its paint scarred from somebody else's war.
She peers from behind a split mooring post, witness notes tucked in her sleeve. Then a familiar voice cracks the cold.
Can just ONE thing go right tonight?!
The Emerald Magistrate, soggy and furious, and a boat, in this freezing cold?
Magistrate-sama!
Gods, are you alright? What in the world happened to you?
A sniffle. A whimper. Tears on wind-reddened cheeks, concern he will not let her offer, and she does not yet know if he is whole.
Bad day for you too, then?
A bad day? Yes. Yes, it has been a bad day!
Calamity and hunger and suffering, and that spooky nonsense in the wards, and now you, you almost sank a boat, and it is so cold, and you could have died...
I'm fine, To-chan. Just cold.
...why are you even out here in a boat?
There's no other way to reach Teardrop Island. Obviously.
Stand there gawking or come warm me. It has been a bad day, To-chan, and you are the only fire on this pier.
Yes, Magistrate-sama.
I am not cargo to haul around on your bad night.
Crane spine, even on a frozen pier. Brave. Foolish. Mine either way.
Then ask. Do not order. Not when you need me.
I asked with the boat and the bay. And you are still here, aren't you.
Almost enough. But not quite.
The deck of a boat is not a tatami mat.
Worse.
Knees, hips, shoulder, wet wood. Pain and surprise in one breath. The rock of the boat is wrong, almost dizzying.
You are on top today. I am too cold to manage you, and you have feelings to work through besides. Get to it. File them on my hull.
O-oh. Alright then.
The hull rocks. His palms brace the gunwales whenever the boat threatens to tip. Good girl, breathed against her hair, implied, never filed, a hunger the ledger has no column for.
When the rhythm ends, they are a knot of warmth and borrowed robes. Bay cold waits outside the strakes.
...You didn't, though. You didn't find me.
I found you. Do you remember?
Hm? Oh. I suppose that is true. Were you really looking for someone like me, though?
I went looking for a magistrate to handle my paperwork. But I found Kitsu Kaoru, the man.
I keep wondering what I did to deserve the one witness who lets a man like me bully her toward the warm side of the boat.
Your color is coming back. Can we please go home now?
Fiiiiiiiine.
A bath, and mikan under the kotatsu. That is the treaty.
Toa-san? Next time I will have you again behind my screen, in a proper bath, where the bay cannot watch. The marina was never the place for it.
They ferry back before the watch invents a drowning. Steam and citrus in the magistrate wing, bath, kotatsu, mikan peeled in silence that is almost domestic.
Case Five will not wait just because you bruised your knees on my kobune.
Yes, Magistrate-sama. The witness line is written.
And To-chan, do your sulking in private if you must. The marina saw quite enough of us tonight.
Case Five begins when the pleasure-quarter seal goes missing. Until then, witness notes sleep, not romance.
The file line is written. I am still at your door.
Dawn through cedar shutters. Duplicate charter cooling on the desk; tea steaming; the outer clerk already transferred to a cell.
The Academy thinks you're still respectable. I think you're still mine to complicate.
Respectable until noon, then. The rest of me is already yours.
Tea cools untouched on the desk. They stay wrapped in the same cushion warmth instead, his thumb on her knuckle, her forehead against his shoulder, neither willing to break the spell first.
Tsubaki deserved a better city. I deserved not to lose my future in ash.
You kept both. That is rarer than virtue here.
Don't make me used to mornings that don't hurt.
Too late. Case Three will hurt worse. I'll be beside you when it does, if you keep choosing me over the door.
The door can wait. The tea can't.
Then punish me, Magistrate-sama. You have been holding that threat over me since the night I touched the wrong door. So use it.
You demand my desk in front of a half-drowned clerk and a Miya witness. That was stupid, To-chan. It was also the moment you stopped being anyone else's.
I did not mean... I only thought you would never actually...
...would never dare. Go on, keep guessing.
My office. My corridor. We are finished when I say the word, not when your nerve runs out.
Rain beads on the canal rope. The clerk studies his wax tablet. Kaoru's hand closes on her elbow, escort, not comfort, and the compound swallows them.
You begged for closed screens twice in one night. Congratulations. You will have them.
Behind closed screens. You heard me perfectly well the first time.
The desk. Now. Before you confuse your appetite for my permission a second time.
An empty witness note. A blank collar line. You have nothing to show me, and you do not get another hour to find it.
Magistrate-sama... let me make one more pass at the canal, please...
The desk. You are about to learn what my hall charges a witness who comes back with nothing to sign.
You wanted theater out on the canal. This office is not a stage, To-chan. It is a desk, a seal, and the consequences of everything you said in front of witnesses.
Magistrate-sama, I am your witness. I am not your...
You are one line on my evening's ledger until I say otherwise. Desk. Now.
Cedar and ink. The docket stack still warm from Case One. His hanko waits beside a narrow custody chit, companion escort, temporary, the kind that buys silence from clerks who learn not to hear.
You pushed me twice at the waterline and once inside my own hall. I gave you the warnings. I do not give them a fourth time.
Let me through... I am not one of your...
You carried my seal's work into Scorpion water and walked back through that gate proud of it. Pride does not survive this room. It bends.
His hand closes on her wrist, not a lover's grip, a magistrate's. Fingers find the pulse the way he finds a misplaced line.
A witness without obedience is just gossip in a clean kosode. Learn the difference faster.
You will knock on my screen again, the night your hunger finally outvotes your pride. Tonight, though, I collect what you owed me back at the canal.
She boards alone, proud, fast, certain the manifest is a prize and not bait.
The factor does not run. He smiles, steps from the awning, and the deckhand's pole finds the small of her back.
Cold canal. Opium-sweet water. The last thing she sees is Scorpion grey paint bubbling under rain.
She walks into the rain, proud, certain the magistrate will call her back before the third bridge.
He does not. The factor's runners do. The companion file closes without her signature.
She lunges alone, pride, Crane footwork, the wish to prove the Academy still owns her blade.
Kurogane's cut is dock work, plain and final, not theater. Rain swallows the pier. The magistrate's file closes without her breath.
She fights the throw, Crane pride against a hull built for fishermen. Shoulder and ribs meet the thwart wrong. Breath leaves. The kobune keeps rocking as if it did not witness.
Bandages. Rain on shoji. A magistrate's shadow at the marina pilings that does not cross the gunwale, as if grief might be contagious on a ledger.
The hospital cart creaks toward the lower quarter. Ryoko Owari keeps its boats. It does not always keep its dancers.
She enters the kiln alley ahead of him, ash in her palms, proof in her mouth, pride in her stride.
The clerk's knife was not for Kaoru. It was for the dancer who would not let the Academy packet stay dead.
Tsubaki's ghost gets company. Toa's charter burns with the rest.
The roll catches her shoulder, then the mat, then the world tilts wrong. Crane footwork is not armor against a room built to kill witnesses.
Bandages. Rain on shoji. A magistrate's shadow in the doorway that does not cross the threshold, as if grief might be contagious on a ledger.
The hospital cart creaks toward the canal quarter. Ryoko Owari keeps its books. It does not always keep its dancers.
Outside, the canal district smells honest, fish, copper, rain on stone.
Down the canal road the lanterns bleed orange into black water. Copper and cheap incense, wet stone and old smoke, Ryoko Owari breathing on the back of her neck.
Scorpion country doesn't shout. It watches a soaked Crane girl splash past, decides she is no one worth a second glance, and lets the rain do the rest.
No seal. No patron. No permit that means anything. By morning a gate guard asks for paper, and I have a wet book and a very good bow.
She slows where the lamplight gives out. Past it the city is only rain and the shape of rain.
She kept her pride. She picked it up off the magistrate's desk, whole, and carried it out under her arm. Tonight it is the only thing she owns in Ryoko Owari.
...Snacks first. Pride second. I finally got the order right.
Pity there was never a third.
The lamplight ends. What is left is rain on white hair and a bow that will not hold.
On stage she could make grief look graceful. Here there is no audience, only the canal breathing back her own shaking.
Crane don't... Crane don't break in public.
Mother taught me the spine first. The smile second. I kept both until tonight.
She presses her forehead to the permit book. The paper is pulp. The crane on the obi is the only thing still dry enough to pretend it flies.
Three provinces of ink, and not one line that says I may sleep indoors.
She tries to flatten the pages with her palm. The rain wins. Somewhere a magistrate's hanko dries by his stove while she dissolves on a corner stone.
A side alley mouths open between two shuttered tea houses, dry enough to stand, narrow enough to trap.
She stumbles in to wipe her face. Her reflection in a puddle is a stranger's, smaller, older, already bargaining.
Boots scrape stone behind her. Two ronin, hired by the cut of their silence, not the color of their haori.
I'm Kakita. I'm not inventory.
Touch me and I'll memorize your face for when I'm allowed a sword again.
A hand on her shoulder. Another on the permit book, tearing it free like spoiled fruit.
Please... the book... that's all I...
She twists. Crane training was for stages and polite duels, not alley brawls. They have the numbers. She has pride, and pride does not block three men.
A fist in her obi. A gag that tastes of cheap sake and river mud.
The alley becomes a cart under oilcloth. The cart becomes a door that smells of incense too sweet to be prayer, rouge and bruised plums and someone else's laughter behind thin walls.
They write her name the way the city writes drowning: not on a funeral stone, but on a ledger line.
Kakita Toa will not be asked to sign it.
Morning after Case Two's ash still clings to the duplicate charter. The outer bell rings with cloth, not blood, a bolt merchant's runner with a seal that smells of Scorpion wax.

Case Three. That Chrysanthemum factor from Case One did not drown with his barge after all. His cousin sells kimono behind a borrowed Crane name, and the bolt counts never quite agree with the tax lines.
Fabric instead of dead men in canals. That is almost civilized, Magistrate-sama.
Civilized is how this city hides its knives. You wanted a witness note that outlives the clerks who file it. Earn it in the bolt room, or lose it on my desk.
You sleep on the other side of my office wall now. So today you walk the shop at my side. Not ahead of me, not alone.
I heard every word at the festival. Surely Case Three can wait until the tea cools.
The tea cooled yesterday. The file did not.
Your permit survived Case Two. Case Three decides whether a single soul in the Academy still believes your name means anything.
If the bolts lie on paper, the shelves lie in the room. I want the numbers before I want any names.
Numbers before names. The Academy did teach you something after all. Bring me a line I can paste straight into the file without crossing out half your adjectives.
A clerk lies with his mouth and tells the truth with his hands. I will watch both.
Discipline. Good. Ask him who profits when a bolt room happens to collapse on a Crane witness.
Chrysanthemum patron, a forged writ, now silk. Someone keeps braiding Case One straight into my obi.
Then do not braid poetry on my desk to match. Tag it, bag it, witness it.
The shop smells of camphor and indigo vat. Bolts lean like sleeping courtiers; paper tags flutter when the street door breathes. A clerk in Crane colors bows too low, smile too fast.
Magistrate's custody. Open the bolt room. No one lays a finger on the top shelf until my witness has signed the count.
The third bell has not even rung, and this clerk is already sweating through his Crane collar. He is afraid of the room, Magistrate-sama, not of us.

Because someone wanted the inventory to come down the moment the right person stood beneath it. Ask your questions. I will be at the street door. Close enough to hear you scream, far enough that the clerks still think you are alone.
You are leaving me alone in the aisle.
I am handing you a clerk who will talk to a dancer and lie to a magistrate. Use that.
Crimson tagged Crane on the outside; inside thread, the six-legged mark of a Scorpion factor's private vat. Someone swapped labels before the tax count.
This bolt belongs in Case One's file, not on some merchant's shelf.
His hands shake when she asks for wax. A thin book appears, night counts that do not match the day book Kaoru will seize at the door.
You signed two different truths. Decide now which one drowns when the magistrate reads them both.
The brace shows a clean saw kerf beneath old lacquer, deliberate, recent. The top shelf lists a finger's width toward the aisle.
This isn't a storeroom. It's a deadfall someone stacked with silk.
The clerk excuses himself for 'fresh seals.' The street door latches. Somewhere above, rope groans, too much weight on too fresh a cut.
A lantern sways. The top bolt shifts, pale silk unrolling like a white serpent, shelf timber screaming.
The shelf goes. Silk hammers air; dust becomes snow. Toa has one breath and two bad choices, call the man at the door, or prove Crane training still wins alone.
He was already moving, not at the street door, but inside the line of fall, magistrate coat thrown back, one arm hooked under her obi.
They hit the mat together sideways, silk brushing her cheek, his breath hot at her temple, heartbeat louder than the clerk's lies.
Up. Now. Before that clerk invents a story where you died clumsy.
You... your hands are shaking.
A draft, from the alley. Nerves. Stand.
For one heartbeat his grip does not loosen. Grey eyes on hers, too honest, stripped of performance.
If that shelf had taken you, there would be no bolt room left. No quarter. Nothing but the canal and my apology to it.
Magistrate-sama...
Forget I said that. Witness note: shelf sabotage, clerk detained. You are breathing. That is the only romance this file requires.
I am not, that is not what, I-I will write the shelf line first.
Good. Devotion stays on paper until I say otherwise.
She twists, Crane footwork in a space built for merchants, not dancers. Pride says the roll misses. Physics disagrees.
By afternoon the clerk has named the Chrysanthemum cousin's runner, the runner has named a shelf payment, and Kaoru inks a custody chit thick enough to survive one jealous factor.
Case Three is not closed. It is pinned. Like the bolt that almost killed my witness.
The mistagged lot ties straight back to Case One's flower. Good. Paste that line into the file before some Scorpion lawyer buys the clerk's silence.
Someone paid good money for that saw kerf. I want the name that signed for the brace, not the boy who only held the saw.
I still hear the shelf coming down every time I close my eyes. Thank you for, for being at the door.
I was at the mat, not the door. Do not make poetry of it. Case Four will knock soon enough, the moment the rain comes back.
Case Three's first file line is written. The city still lies, but she is still breathing in Ryoko Owari.
The fabric-shop clerk's runner never reached the canal office. A dock watchman swears he fled toward the lower piers with Case Three's night ledger, grey wax still wet on the cord.
Case Four is where the paper trail runs out and the steel begins. We raid the lower dock tonight. Bring me Kurogane, or bring me his blood.
Magistrate-sama, I'm a witness. Not a yoriki.
Tonight you are both. Stay in my line, or the file learns that you didn't.

Rain hammers the compound before dawn. Case Three's custody chit is barely dry when Kaoru pins a dock watchman's note beside the bolt-room saw kerf. Lower pier. Warehouse three. A foreman who signs his name in unmarked grey, Scorpion-trained under the lacquer.
Case Four. Kurogane runs the split crates our clerk ran toward. He learned his trade under a Scorpion quartermaster, so he will not surrender to a brush and ink.
And me? Another bolt room to comb through, or steel this time?
Steel. You dance with a blade when I tell you to dance. You do not duel a foreman on your own.
You learned how to breathe in my bolt room. Tonight you breathe in my line, or the ledger learns that you couldn't.
Magistrate-sama, I am not your decoration.
Correct. You are a witness with a wakizashi. Walk like you know the difference.
Lower piers, tar ropes, split crates, wrong-green canal breath. Lanterns gutter in rain. The warehouse mouth swallows sound.
Three breaths. Read the room. Then we take him.
Grey wax, the sixteen-petal Imperial seal again, the same forger's hand from Case One. He didn't drown with that barge. He just changed warehouses.
Note that down before the steel starts talking.
Foreman Kurogane. Scorpion pay, Crane crates for cover. He bolted the moment the clerk did.
Good. Say his name again when his blade clears the sheath.
The stairs are mine. You take the floor. I won't break formation.
Discipline, with the steel this close. I will take it.
Kurogane! Emerald custody. Lower your blade, or lower your head.
[case4_suspect_name]! Emerald custody. Lower your blade, or lower your head.
A foreman steps from crate shadow, katana already drawn, rain streaming off Scorpion-trained shoulders. He does not bow.
Then talk to my witness note. After you sheathe that blade.
Three blades in rain, Kaoru's katana a clean arc, Toa's dance-line wakizashi, Kurogane's Scorpion cut trying to split them. Crate wood splinters. Footing is blood-slick tar.
Toa! Hold the line!
Kurogane feints high, drops low, steel aimed at her ribs, not his. One breath. Crane footwork or magistrate's shadow.

She drops back a single step, but not into his shadow. Her wakizashi rides the dance-line up and turns the foreman's low cut a hand's width wide, just long enough. Kaoru crosses into the opening she bought him, and his coat takes the edge that would have opened her ribs.
Steel screams once. Kurogane stumbles, custody rope, not mercy. Kaoru's sleeve is dark with rain or worse; his free hand still finds her wrist, pinning her behind his shoulder.
Breathe. Count to three. That deflection was clean. The Academy would not believe me if I filed it honestly.
I bought you one breath and you spent it shielding me. We could have both stood, Magistrate-sama.
If you had died on my dock, I would have burned this whole pier down to the canal. I am not going to pretend I did not say it this time.
Forget I said it. Witness note: foreman detained, ledger seized. You are still breathing, and that is the only romance the file requires tonight.
I am not, that is not... I will write up the blade line first.
She lunges, pride, Crane training, the wish to prove the Academy still owns her footwork. Kurogane's cut is not a performance. It is a dockman's arithmetic.
By dawn the foreman's manifest sits in custody beside Case Three's saw kerf. The clerk's runner has not vanished, only gone quiet, which in Ryoko Owari is its own confession.
Case Four is pinned, not closed. The flower still has its roots.
You stayed in my line when the steel wanted you alone. Do not expect applause. Expect a pleasure-quarter seal stolen by morning.
I stayed because the file said witness. Not because...
Because is a word for Case Five. Tonight you sleep.
Case Four's line is written. The city still lies, but I am still at your door.
Witness is a word for paper that has not earned ink yet. Case Five opens at the hour of the serpent. Dress for court, not for my corridor.
We are talking about them. In a room that can hear you.
Leave the adjoining chamber key at the gate. Today you are witness. The hall does not care what you called last night.
Good. That pleasure-quarter seal on the summons is bait for clerks who think Case Five is only Chrysanthemum politics. It is not. Stay in my line.
Case One, you read a lie under pressure at the Lacquered Plum and you did not run when the comb turned out to be Scorpion.
Case Two, you stood on the hill where the city could see you beside my file, and you did not hide behind Crane honor when kiln ash choked the alley.
Case Three, you trusted the bolt room when the room tried to kill you. You let me pull you out instead of proving the Academy right on splinters.
Case Four, you stayed behind my shoulder when steel wanted you alone. You did not compose poetry on my dock.
I said provisional attachment until the files close. They were real cases, and they did not close themselves, To-chan. I was not testing you. I was watching what each one revealed.

I meant a left hand. The city needs a name on it. I could not offer it behind my screen, or the quarter would call it a kept woman's wages. You had to be seen choosing the desk over the road. Forgive the cold morning. I chose your name before you knew what the job was called.
Kitsu Kaoru, Emerald Magistrate. Case Five: witness chains for the Chrysanthemum root, and appointment of sworn yoriki for the ongoing docket.
Witness is not enough in this city. You signed my corridor, my cushion, my release. Let the quarter whisper kept woman. The file will say office.
Kakita Toa. Appointment as yoriki to the Emerald office of Ryoko Owari. Witness chains, quarter escort, left-hand signature on my docket.
You have already served this desk. You slept behind my screen. You argued well every time I needed a sharp mind within reach.
This is office. I am not asking for poetry. I need a name the city can cite when the seal walks.
You passed every case I put in front of you. Do not make me say it twice in front of clerks who sell courage by the cup.
Speak without the docket listening. One sentence you never filed, and one debt you still owe my desk.
I know.
Most people try to rename me. You let me keep you, and still walked back to my corridor on your own feet.
Then stand. The oath is public. The rest is mine to file when you stop stammering like a petitioner.
Still mine. That is the only title that matters behind my screen tonight.
File the witness chain before noon. The Chrysanthemum root still has tendrils in the pleasure quarter.
Good. Case Five is pinned, not closed. The city still lies.
You served the docket. The city has your testimony. Do not expect my corridor to keep a room warm on gratitude alone.
Good. Case Five sleeps on my desk until someone earns the left hand. The Chrysanthemum root keeps its tendrils in the quarter, the way the big files always do.
You refused the name. The city will still want one on my left hand. It will not be yours.
Then I will not forge your hand onto a docket you refuse to stand on. An oath taken under pressure is just another counterfeit seal, and I have hanged men for those.
Your permit stands, dated and honest. The stipend closes with the case. The adjoining chamber empties tonight. Dance in any quarter that will have you, and none of them will owe me a thing.
Scroll ink dries at the dais. You are not at the dais anymore.
Temporary escort. Left hand filled. Her name stays off my appointment scroll.
Fine. The hall keeps what the scroll would have claimed. Holding cell. Ink. Witnesses who learn not to hear.
You are a Crane dancer who embarrassed my docket in open court. The file will say corrective custody.
Thumb here. Or I file you as flight risk and let the runners collect.
The quarter keeps what I sell. You keep what you refused to price.
Corrective custody closes at dawn. What happens before dawn is hall business.
Clerks sell courage by the cup. You sell me indignation by the segment.
Almost is the only concession this office allows before sunset.
Eat your mikan. Drip on the yoriki sash and I will make you copy the stain into the record twice. I still take what I am owed.
Just this room is still mine to share when the city is not listening. Do not make me say it twice.
Magistrate-sama, the runner would not meet my eyes. Does that mean the witness line is finished?
Court sounds like dismissal. Or punishment. You said when the files closed we would talk about terms.
Then I will attend as your witness one last time. The hall taught me how to stand where I am told.
You never told me any of that was a test.
I thought you meant stipend. A permit. A room next to yours.
Yoriki is a sworn magistrate's rank. That is not the same as a dancer's permit.
Magistrate-sama, Crane custom expects an honor guard and clan auditors at my side. Not a magistrate's toy left on a public desk.
I accept the appointment and its duties. You will have my discretion and my attendance.
I will not embarrass your file.
I needed the permit to stay close, but I chose to stay on purpose. I could have run. Then you could have caught me.
You are not easy.
Behind your screen I can be yours to keep. In the hall I do not want to be carried in your file. I want to stand.
Magistrate-sama, still yours.
Yes, Magistrate-sama. The line is written, and I am still at your door.
I will not ask for more than you owe the file.
Magistrate-sama, please.
I am Kakita Toa of the Crane. I came for a permit, not to become a name the city cites when the seal walks.
Magistrate-sama... I will sign. I will take the oath...
...Not like this...
I am not a Scorpion debtor you can cage for sport.
I... Magistrate-sama, this is not...
Yoriki paperwork says I must initial every quarter escort in triplicate. Your clerks invented a fourth copy while I bathed.
I am teasing. You may almost smile if you try.
Good. I will file that under victories too small for the docket.
No new case tonight. No seal stolen before dawn. Just this room.
Then I will stay where the ledger cannot count.
