Counting is witness work. Stop filing ceiling beams and sleep.
I did not ask for a chambermate either, and yet here you are. Drink before it goes cold. I am not thanking you for tea I did not request.
Thank you would admit I wanted the company. I wanted a body in my corridor who could read a ledger without fainting. Different line item.
The corridor is still mine. The blanket is only a loan against your noise. Snore, and I reassign you to the archive.
Good night, To-chan. Case One starts at dawn. Be vertical. Scheduling, not romance.
The kitchen is not a courtroom, To-chan. Neither is the lid of that pot.
Official lentils are still lentils. Put my chop on paper, not on my dinner. I am not signing your gratitude into the pot lid.
Edible. More than I can say for the Academy letters out on the desk. Case Two has been waiting there since this morning.
I ate the proof that you follow instructions when you are not stamping dinner. Do not expect a second serving or a softer inventory.
And you are still in my corridor. That is filing enough for one afternoon. Try not to walk like a woman carrying a secret she forgot to seal.
If you are awake over there, you are doing a terrible job of hiding it. The whole city can hear you pacing.
I brought you tea. I know you did not ask for any.
You still have not said thank you, you know.
Then I will file my breathing under acceptable noise. Good night, Magistrate-sama.
Case One is closed, and you survived a whole tray of my handwriting. So today I am cooking you thank-you curry, not filing a report about it.
I was only lining up the seal. A proper hanko makes everything official, does it not?
Then they can keep waiting until I have washed the pot. You did finish the whole bowl, I noticed.
Kitchen seal noted, then. Case Two is next, and I am still right here at your door.
Filed. And I promise I will not stamp the ladle again.
Do not perform stillness at me, To-chan. I have read quieter ledgers than the one your body is keeping tonight.
The archive sleeps. You do not. Hands on the post. Do not leave a mark I cannot explain.
Quiet. Take what I give you from behind the screen and do not drip on my tatami. I know what I am paying for.
Magistrate-sama, the archive will hear you.
Tea is witness work when someone wants a favor. File the cup. I did not ask.
Gratitude in liquid form is still a bid. I do not accept bids before breakfast.
You may leave the second if it saves you a walk. I still will not drink gratitude.
If you want to please me, bring dry copies and leave the sugar on someone else's tray.
Three mornings, three cups, zero admissions. When the dancer arrives with tea she will learn the same arithmetic.
Mikan comes later. Peel on a tray. Domestic filing. I will deny that too until the quarter stops selling what I intend to keep.
When the archive boy brought mikan peel on a tray. Denied.
When Witness ████ cried thank-you on the stairs and bowed too low. Denied.
When the puppet villain on the canal road got the children to clap. Denied.
When the rain stopped for six breaths and the office went quiet enough to pretend this city was kind. Denied.
When the night clerk laughed at my stamp and called me handsome in a voice that wanted a corridor pass. Denied.
When the okami's runner bowed with coin already counted and called me merciful. Denied. Merciful is a word witnesses use before they learn the price.
When I thought of a kotatsu and wool and citrus and a mouth that might ask me to almost smile on purpose. Denied twice. Denied in advance.
Paper first. Mouth later. If later ever comes.
Watching is free. Smiling is a debt I have not agreed to owe.
Next stair. Do not wait for praise.
If you linger I will deduct a coin for theater.
Run.
Wrong motive. He killed for debt schedule, not passion. Ledger line due on the fifteenth. Wife already sold the comb.
Puppeteer, your villain emotes well and files poorly. Fear is cheaper than love in this quarter. Write that on your crate.
Dancers make the same mistake. Pretty feet, wrong reason. I will know the difference when one knocks.
Sponsorship is not kindness. It is a calendar and a corridor and a body I intend to read like a docket.
When the renewal petition comes I will not be the villain in purple. I will be the stamp. That is scarier and more honest.
Street theater is not my docket unless it blocks my corridor.
Citation keeps the puppeteer honest and the children moving. File it.
Wrong quarter to be visible without my seal.
I could open the watch door. I could write you a corridor pass until dawn.
Instead I will close the other door.
You wanted my corridor. This is what my corridor costs when I do not lend it.
Witness spendable when the quarter pays better. Patronage is appetite with a stamp. I know what I am buying.
I could have opened the watch door. I chose the fee line. Do not call that romance. Call it jurisdiction.
Case Zero closes. Next petition lands when some Crane gets lost in my hall.
Renewal season. Wrong door season. I will drink none of the tea and take all of the witness.
Companion means my corridor, my hanko, my release. I wrote that line before she existed. I intend to fill the blank.
Almost-smile stays denied. The corridor stays mine.
Corridor's awake. Renewal season.
She will knock wrong first. They always do.
Come back when you learn my corridor. You will.
Come back when you learn my corridor. You will.
Before I read it aloud, one question. Plainly. When your permit was dying, you danced for me in this room. The quarter forgets dancers who vanish after sunset. I don't.
You watched like the whole city had gone quiet. That was not a clerk's audition, Magistrate-sama.
No. Witnesses lie. You had a body worth housing and a voice worth putting on a filing.
What do you actually want from me? Not the polite version. The one you write down on paper.
Attendance. Discretion. Art that doesn't embarrass the seal on my door.
If you need proof, I'll dance. Not for ink this time. For your eyes only.
Later. First you hear what I'm willing to pay for.
I came for a renewal, not a collar. Tell me what this costs before I seal anything.
Brave. The cost is written right here. Listen.
This is sponsorship, not a courtesan's contract. The ledger reads art donor to artist. I will not insult your lord or mine by playing danna to a Crane who crossed provinces for ink.
Sponsorship. Not... not that.

Coin for your art, openly given. I know exactly what I am paying for, and so do you. 'Patronage' is the courtesy the ledger requires. Interpret it as liberally as you like, so long as you do it under my roof.
How often, Magistrate-sama? And where? The thirtieth was supposed to mean residency, not...
Twice a week you attend me here. For performance, and for case work when I need a witness who doesn't flinch. The rest is written below.
Then we arrive the way the law arrives. Seal out, comb wrapped, nothing hidden. Let the okami count what we already hold.
Seal on the desk, comb in plain cloth. Crude, but the Plum opens for whatever it can see.
Send me in through the kitchen first. I spent three years smiling at tired women in painted rooms. They'll tell a dancer what they'd never tell your seal.
Your past, turned into a bargaining chip. I dislike how useful it keeps being.
Go in soft. I'll follow once the room is warm. Don't enjoy it more than the case.
You knock. I'll read the faces behind you. Safer for everyone that way.
Finally. Stand where I point. Breathe when I allow it. The Plum mistakes quiet witnesses for furniture, so use that.
Suzu. Sit. Breathe. You're not betraying him by saying it. You're the only funeral he's ever going to get.
Suzu, the river didn't take Jiro. Fingers did. I saw the marks myself, dark as plum skin under his jaw. You saw them too. Didn't you.
A manifest worth a man's throat. Twice over.
She gave that to fear, not to us. Remember that before you call it a victory.
She'll talk while she's frightened. Ask now, before the okami buys her courage back.
Let it be witnessed. A false Emerald seal locked this room the night Miya Jiro was murdered inside it. The okami heard me. The factor heard me. The river does not get this one.
You said it aloud, against my instruction and your own safety both. The Crane envoy won't laugh now. Neither will the Scorpion.
Reckless. Effective. You've put the forgery on the okami's ledger, where no drowning can erase it.
I'll trace the petals onto rice paper and set the book back exactly where it lay. Let whoever cut that false seal sleep easy one more night, just long enough to lead us home.
Patience over theater. The Chrysanthemum keeps his appointment, and we keep the advantage. Good.
It's your mark and your jurisdiction, Magistrate-sama. I'll carry it wherever you point, and save my questions for where the walls don't lean in to listen.
You're learning the shape of safety at my side. The factor sees it too. Watch him reconsider the door.
Wise. In this quarter, the only seal worth standing behind is the one that frightens factors. Behind me. Now.
Rain, rope shadows, and a dancer's feet. I'll be on that deck before they finish counting heads.
Theft as a craft. I approve, provided you steal the right ledger page.
Emerald seal in hand. They can surrender the manifest, or explain it to the Champion's auditors.
Loud. Honest. Try not to get yourself shot before I've finished enjoying their faces.
You make the noise. I'll make the copy. That's a division of labor I can trust.
Finally. A companion who understands spectacle as cover.
Watch from the gangplank if you must. The manifest is mine to take.
Toa. That deck is full of the flower's men, and his hand has already strangled one clerk this season. Step onto it alone and you are the next name the canal swallows. Do not.
A clerk who couldn't even earn a funeral, clerking in a pleasure house.
The okami won't open her registry for a watchman. She might open it for a magistrate. Give her no reason to lie faster than she already means to.
You walk a half step behind me, and you speak only when I open the door. The quarter swallows companions who forget who lights the lanterns.
Half a step. The written terms said escort, not muzzle.
In the Plum, the muzzle and the escort are the same thing. Stay where I can see you.
Half a step behind the most feared man in the noble quarter. I think I can live with that.
Flatter the okami like that and she'll tip her whole ledger into your lap.
You're not my hand yet. In the Plum you're a witness I tolerate. Try tolerating me back.
Tolerance, then. It's somewhere to start.
Snacks after paperwork. Does the Lacquered Plum count as paperwork, or as the field?
It counts as a hunt. Now decide how we knock.
The air's thin again. Peeled-charm thin. Someone scrubbed protection off this doorway and never bothered to replace it.
Or never wanted one. The Plum prefers guests unwatched by anything that reports upward.
And yet you kept Miya Jiro. He clerked your registry until the canal kept him instead. I want the book he wrote in.
Respectable houses survive by knowing which silences cost more than others. This silence will cost you the Plum itself. Choose.
Afraid of what?
A flower alias, foreign silver, frightened clerks. Suzu's mouth next, before the okami buys her silence back.
She's a frightened girl with one true thing left in her mouth. Get it out before her courage spends itself. How?
Booked, paid, private. And here, that's Jiro's hand. The third-bell delivery, signed off the very night he died.
Magistrate-sama, look at the seal. This chrysanthemum has sixteen petals. The Emerald office only ever cuts fourteen. The stamp's a forgery. A fine one, but the petal count gives it away.

Sixteen petals. The forger did not merely counterfeit my office, he reached past it. Sixteen petals is the Emperor's own chrysanthemum. Whoever cut this seal dressed a smuggling cover in the Imperial mon, which makes it treason, and used it to lock a room where a Crane clerk was strangled inside my jurisdiction.
That's your office's mark, isn't it? An Emerald writ, sealing the river room off private the night Jiro died.
It is my office's mark. It is not my seal. I authorized no writ for this house all season.
Which leaves me a forgery, or a thief inside the magistracy. Neither one is a comfort.
I am the privilege in this city. Take one step toward that registry, and the watch fishes a second body out of the noble quarter by dawn.
One seal stands between you and that book, and yet here you are, come to fetch it yourself. A truly privileged record wouldn't need collecting by a man who tips in foreign silver.
You came for a book and found a magistrate instead. Tell the Chrysanthemum the Emerald office is missing a seal, and that I've decided to take an interest in flowers.
And a seal cut to wear my mark, sealing the very room he died in. Someone wants this murder to carry the Emerald crest.
We came for a guest registry and found a forger sitting somewhere inside your own office, Magistrate-sama.
You spoke against me twice tonight, and twice you were right. I dislike how much that pleases me. Don't mistake the pleasure for permission.
Then I'll call it progress, and try not to push my luck.
Stubborn. Keep it. I'll need something that doesn't bend when this seal turns out to belong to a man I dine with.
You stood behind me all night and let the quarter break itself against my stillness. That is exactly what a companion of mine is for.
Behind you. Watching. And I still saw the petal count before you did, Magistrate-sama.
You did. Obedient and observant both. I'm beginning to think I kept the right dancer.
Someone tried to hang a murder on my seal. Until I know who, you don't leave this compound without me. Not for the curry shops. Not for Academy letters. Nowhere.
Escort, or cage?
Escort means my corridor, my hanko, my release. Tonight you don't leave without all three.
You're still not sleeping in my hall. But you spoke for the Empire in a Scorpion house tonight, and the wax never once cracked. I'm noting it.
And I'll keep noting it right back, until the ledger reads patronage beside my name.
Survive the Chrysanthemum first. Forgers who cut my seal don't tend to leave their witnesses cheerful.

The Scorpion shipping rolls list one barge on the next high tide, booked to the same chartered concern as the river room. The flower will be aboard, or his manifest will. Either way, we meet the tide.
A forged seal, a barge, and a flower with a strangler's hand. Jiro pointed us up the current. So we follow it.
And it's on the record now. Whoever cut your seal can't drown what a whole house full of witnesses already heard.
And we copied it quiet. The flower books his room one more high tide, never dreaming we traced his petals.
Case One has a name, a comb, and a tide now. Jiro pointed us up the current, and I mean to follow it all the way to the flower.
Chartered concern, false cargo, a flower name on the ledger. Tonight we seize the manifest before the tide signs off on another drowning.
Jiro died for one page in that book. I am not letting the tide take it too.
Stay inside my shadow on the plank. One misstep, and the watch writes up two drownings and calls it efficiency.
They already heard us at the Plum. The barge crew knows we're coming. Good.
You turned a forgery into theater. Now go and finish the play.
You wanted a case. This is the part where the city bites back. Try to keep up.
Magistrate-sama, here's the cargo manifest. Rice in the ledger, resin in the barrels. Jiro was right all along.
A falsified cargo tally. Hold onto that page.
Open the hold. The Emerald office is auditing chartered lies tonight.
False rice tally, true resin weight. Someone taxed the city on its hunger and smuggled poison on the side.
You. The man who threatened my witness. Step into the light.
Got it. Just don't let him swallow the seal this time.
I have enough to hang your chartered concern and every clerk who ever signed for it. Run to your flower. The tide won't hide you twice.
The Chrysanthemum is still a cipher. The factor's concern is not. I'll burn his charter before the week is out.
Jiro gets his name on the watch ledger now, and a line that says strangled. That's a funeral worth standing in the rain for.
And we still have the traced petals from the Plum. The flower has more than one trap waiting for him now.
Academy letters sat on the outer desk all night. Case Two arrived with the dawn, and it isn't a polite one.
Your permit survives because you survived the tide. Case Two is already on the desk. Try not to expect any gratitude.
Case One, closed. Then whatever the city decides to throw at us next.
Rain needles the harbor glass. The parking structure under the licensing tower is a cathedral of dripping concrete, fluorescents buzzing while ferries cough diesel into the channel below.

Ryoko Port keeps its appointments under fluorescent mercy and never apologizes for the weather. The municipal tower hums like a printer that learned to judge people. Floor fourteen B belongs to the Ryoko Port Arts Council, and it was supposed to be the easy part of her morning.
The elevator map said fourteen B. The packet said fast track. Those two facts have not shaken hands yet.

Toa clutches a tablet sleeve, expired sponsorship packet, and the personal stamp she was told to bring to every bureaucratic threshold. Crane logo on her rehearsal jacket, not costume. Ballet flats soaked through anyway.
Wrong conference room. Again.
I wasn't... that is, I'm looking for Arts Council sponsorship intake?

You opened the door to the Office of Arts and Licensing without reading the plate. Intake is the other wing, where applicants wait their turn. This wing is where I decide whether intake wasted its morning. Reading the wrong door is a skill, not an excuse.

On the deputy director's monitor, an Arts Council board member freezes mid-objection. The hearing is live, unmuted, gallery view tiled with councilors and clerks who have never danced for a living. The chat scrolls before she has finished apologizing.
Fine. I'll find a deputy with better signage.

At the Arts Council intake counter two wings over, a junior clerk squints at her packet, circles the expiration date a second time in the same red, and points her back the way she came. Intake takes the form. Intake does not sign it.
Kitsu Kaoru, Deputy Director? That glass door with the badge reader?
Third time's the charm. Or the deputy director. Hopefully both.
Toa straightens her rehearsal jacket, breathes, and tries not to look like a dancer lost in a tax form. Pride and panic share a spine.
Still there? Knock if you want something other than a live Council hearing to fail on the public record.
He does not look up from two monitors until she sits in the chair beside the screen, not the one facing him. Witness posture lives there, he says later. Stage posture dies in the chat.
Crane Conservatory transfer packet. Expired six weeks ago. You walked into my live hearing like a pop-up ad.
The transfer letter said Ryoko Port had a fast track for performing arts sponsorship.
Ryoko Port has a queue. You are in it now, whether you intended to be or not.
Toa kept her hands on her knees and her eyes on the edge of his monitor, where rain smeared the window. Every syllable landed on her spine like a sticker she could not peel off.
Can I at least not be the reason your Zoom looks unprofessional?
You already are. Sit. Witness posture. Not performance posture. I will audit both.

Yellow paper slides across the desk edge in block letters. Do not speak unless prompted. Dates and names only. A second note repeats the difference: witness posture, not performance posture. Someone laughed in a tile and muted themselves. Kaoru unmuted no one.
You want me to audition for a permit extension?
Applicant present for sponsorship review. Packet error is mine to remediate. Continue your agenda item.

When the board member asks whether Arts Council intake sent her, Kaoru says intake sent her to the wrong floor, so he is intake now. That is not comfort. It is jurisdiction, and she discovers she prefers jurisdiction to kindness, because kindness in this port always arrives with an expiration date and a clerk who is not present to be argued with.
I want proof you can follow choreography that is not flirting with clerks. Run the phrase.
That one was clean. You counted out loud.
Again. Less apology in the port de bras.
Counting is witness work. Stop expecting applause from a licensing officer.
Standard rider. Discretion, attendance, and no social posts that tag municipal accounts.
Two riders on the sponsorship draft I am prepared to sign. Pick one before I file you under *disruptive applicant* and let the queue keep you.
Exclusive rehearsal sponsor. After-hours studio access and direct deputy review.
Correct. Boring is enforceable. I can work with boring.

When the hearing ends without praise, he offers a studio key and a hallway that smells of floor wax and rain. The city rents the rehearsal room by the hour to applicants who need to prove they are more than a packet error.
You understand that clause includes my calendar, not romance on letterhead.
That is not a municipal form.
Unless?

Mirror wall. Barre. Rain ticking the glass like a clerk tapping a stamp. She runs the phrase once. Apology still lives in her shoulders. He counts under his breath like a man checking witness notes, not applause.
Building hour passes six. Public elevators sigh into standby. Only the service lift still answers when he badges it, a dull metal box that does not appear on the map tourists photograph.
The contract floor is closed. This floor is not on your calendar. Get in.
Then audit quietly, Deputy Director-sama. The building still has ears.
Rain stripes the glass on the way down. The car shudders once, as if the building cleared its throat. His badge taps the reader on a floor that does not appear on the public map.
They don't give case numbers upstairs. So today I am cooking thank-you curry, not filing a report about it.
Quiet. You wanted exclusive rehearsal. I audit deliverables.
I brought the stamp. A proper hanko makes everything official, does it not?
The break room is not a courtroom. Neither is the lid of that pot.

She does not perform purity afterward. Whatever the service lift was, every form that matters will still call it sponsorship, after-hours rehearsal access logged under a rider she signed with her eyes open. The seal stays professional on paper. The rest stays off the public record, where the exclusive rider keeps it.

Next midday. The municipal break room smells of curry roux and a little guilt. Fluorescents hum. Rain keeps filing itself against the window. Somewhere upstairs a printer jams and someone swears with the tenderness of a prayer.
Official lentils are still lentils. Put my chop on paper, not on your paper plate.
Filed. And I promise I will not stamp disposable tableware again.
Three business days effective. Do not perform gratitude on municipal letterhead.
He eats without praise and without flinching, as though his jurisdiction now extends to broth. Toa watches his chopsticks and tries not to hope too visibly.
See that you don't. The queue remembers applicants who treat stamps like confetti.
Then I'll file my breathing under acceptable noise. Good night, Deputy Director-sama.

The sponsorship contract returns to her tablet sleeve with a fresh effective date. Three business days. Not a love letter. Still binding. She reads the effective line twice because numbers are safer than whatever lives in her chest when he stands too close in an elevator.
Blanket is a loan against your noise. Snore, and I reassign you to the public waiting area.
You almost smiled when I said thank-you curry, didn't you?
Peel one. Domestic filing. I will deny that too until the port stops selling what I intend to keep.
Motion denied. Good night, To-chan.
After hours, his office couch accepts two people who still call it sponsorship on every form that matters. Harbor lights smear across the window.
Clementines on the armrest, bright as small suns he will deny noticing. Shared blanket. Almost-smile inventory: denied, pending, denied again.
Mandatory on-site witness for a surprise inspection. That sounds like a field trip with liability.
Floor fourteen B is still the wrong door tomorrow. Try reading the plate first.

The wellness corridor is a row of Council-licensed calm: massage studios, float tanks, candle rhetoric under one neon awning, every storefront holding an operating license his office issued. Deputy Director Kitsu Kaoru walks like the queue is already behind him.
Velvet Lantern Wellness Collective. The sign promises serenity in four fonts.

Their operating license promises posted occupancy, working fire exits, and honest books. My inspection confirms it, or my office pulls the license. The witness log needs a sponsor artist on it. That is you.
Harbor mist and pink neon turn the wet sidewalk into a brochure nobody asked for.
Surprise inspection. No appointment. If they scrub the lobby, we note the scrub.
His clipboard is municipal grey. Her phone is personal black. Both will end up in the same PDF.
Do I film everything or only what you point at?
You film what I tell you is exhibit-worthy. Flirt with the lens on your own time.
The front desk host smiles like a man who has never seen a deputy director before noon.
Operating entity on file: Scorpion-grey Holdings LLC. Cute. File that under *names that audition for subpoenas*.
Is that a problem or a punchline?
It is a line item. Grey LLCs love grey corridors. We walk them anyway.
Toa bites her cheek so she does not laugh in a room that already smells like eucalyptus and panic.
Witness protocol. Choose how you document before I choose for you.
Timestamped video. If they move a chair, the chair has a timecode.
Good. Bureaucracy loves clocks. So do I, when they save me a hearing.
Typed log. Quiet thumbs. No flash.
Also acceptable. Do not typo my name. I will notice.
They move through treatment rooms that are legally not treatment rooms until the inspector says otherwise.
Form 14-C requires posted capacity. Count the candles as people and I will cite you for poetry.
Fourteen seats, twelve candles, one diffuser working overtime.
Write *diffuser exceeds serenity*. That is flirtation via footnote, To-chan, and I allow it once.
You called me To-chan in a wellness closet. Is that witness work or harassment?
It is scheduling. You respond faster when I use the nickname inventory.
Her phone buzzes with a calendar ping she is not allowed to open during an active inspection.
The floor manager finds them at the aromatherapy storage door. His badge says *Director of Calm*.
You are interrupting a Council inspection of a license this office issued and this office can revoke. Step aside, or join the exhibit list.
Deputy Director Kitsu is on record. I am on record. Your hallway is on record.
The manager's smile dies in a very professional way.
We only need five more minutes and your posted capacity chart. Sponsorship requires patience.
She said patience. I said compliance. Both are true. Move.
He moves. The corridor exhales eucalyptus and defeat.
For ten seconds the hallway is only rain on glass, clipboard metal, and a man deciding whether calm is a job title or a threat.
You wanted firm. He learned firm. Log the timestamp.
Logged. My hands shook. That is also on the record.
Shaking is human. Falsifying is not. Continue.
Back at the tower, the inspection closes without blood, without bodies, and with three minor citations the Council will post as politely worded threats against a storefront's operating license.
You passed witness work. That is not a compliment. It is a classification.
I'll take classifications that keep my sponsorship active.

There is a harbor weekend on the calendar, logged as an audit retreat. Continued witness work: your clause, my signature, the Council's letterhead. Ferry slips Saturday. One bed in the Airbnb filing is a clerical error I will not fix unless you ask in writing.
That sounds like Case 2 with salt air.
It sounds like a calendar invite. Accept on the municipal portal or argue with the tide.
The service elevator remembers them from the wrong-floor building. Rain stripes the glass. Proximity becomes paperwork if you stare at it long enough.
Unless the harbor?
Unless the harbor. Not romance on letterhead.
Correct. File that under rider compliance.
Their reflections almost touch in the glass. Neither reaches. The lift dings like a stamp.
Saturday on the harbor ferry schedule is a suggestion. Rain owns the channel. Kakita Toa owns a duffel bag and a Council sponsorship rider that still says *not romance on letterhead*.
Deputy Director Kitsu Kaoru owns the calendar invite, the Airbnb confirmation, and the expression of a man who has already filed the weather as exhibit A.
If the ferry is late, do we still owe the island a witness log?
You owe the island punctuality. The ferry owes us a revised ETA. Those are different dockets.
The terminal roof drips into puddles that reflect diesel and regret. Commuters complain in the polite register of people who will not get refunds.
Two hours late. My tracksuit is waterproof. My patience is municipal.
Patience is a line item. Stand where I can see you and the manifest.
When the ferry finally coughs to the pier, salt air replaces toner. Toa stops apologizing in her shoulders without being told.
The harbor Airbnb is cedar shingles, one parking space, and a lockbox that thinks it is a deputy director.
Cute. Very *audit retreat*. Does the listing mention ghosts or only damp towels?
It mentions one queen bed, one sofa, and a clerical error I will not fix unless you ask in writing.
Inside, the rental agreement on the tablet glows like a confession booth with Wi-Fi.
One bed. One deputy. That is either a rom-com or a labor violation.
It is a filing. You sleep. I review calendar conflicts. We do not perform couple on the listing photos.
The sofa is narrow. The bed is worse, because it is comfortable and therefore suspicious.
I call the sofa. You call the bed. That is professional roommate energy, right?
Her phone lights up before she can argue with the furniture.
Sango texts: *ferry delay omg*. Then: *one bed airbnb*. Then: *girl is this a date???*
I should tell her it is a harbor audit with a man who counts witness work out loud.
Kaoru does not look at her screen. He looks at her face, which is doing something between laughter and panic.
If you answer *yes*, I will add a footnote: *applicant confuses calendar with courtship*. If you answer *no*, tell the truth in dates and names only.
I text: *not a date. contract says not romance on letterhead. send snacks.*
Good. Now choose how we file the weekend before the island files us.
Roommate mode. Separate sleep surfaces. You keep your blazer on like a seatbelt.
Acceptable. I will deny almost-smile inventory until Monday.
We stress-test the exclusive rider. Not dating. Just... deliverable review with salt air.
You understand that clause is calendar and audit, not romance on letterhead.
She claims the sofa with a blanket fort of municipal dignity. He takes the bed and the laptop, queue numbers reflected in the rain window.
Lights out at eleven. Snore above acceptable noise and I reassign you to the ferry bench.
Then I'll file my breathing under *compliant*. Good night, Deputy Director-sama.
At midnight she hears him typing. At one she hears the rain stop pretending to be subtle. At two she does not cross the room. That is also witness work.
The bed is one surface. The contract is another. Toa stands in the doorway like a woman who has read the rider twice and still wants a third opinion.
Procedural night. Balcony debrief. No deliverables behind closed doors.
Motion granted. Bring your tablet. Leave performance posture in the closet.
After-hours audit. Quiet. Western inn. Not romance on letterhead.
Then audit quietly. The harbor still has ears.
Rain writes shorthand on the window. His blazer folds over the chair like a man who has filed himself for the night. Her tracksuit jacket follows.
Deliverable one. You hold still when I count.
I can hold still. Count.
He audits heat the way he audits queue numbers: thorough, unhurried, denying her the performance of shame.
Deliverable two. You do not perform gratitude on rental linens.
I file gratitude in the break room. You said so.
When she trembles, he steadies her with his palm at her hip and says acceptable noise is still noise.
File it under exclusive rider. Monday calendar owns the rest.
Already filed. Deputy Director-sama.
Sunday night finds them on the balcony with harbor lights smeared across the rail and a tablet open to the municipal portal.
Calendar audit. Ferry back at six. HR block on Tuesday. Answer in dates, not poetry.
Tuesday HR. That sounds like the viral Zoom clip finally grew teeth.

It sounds like signatory pressure. You are listed dependent on the sponsorship I signed. I am the signatory of record. If that clip convinces the Council I favor you, People and Conduct opens a conflict-of-interest file, and the apparatus decides what to do with the pair of us. None of that is romance on letterhead.
She stayed on the sofa. He stayed on the bed. The weekend still felt like proximity wearing a tie.
Roommate mode survived. Barely. Sango will not believe me.
Her neck still remembers counting. His voice stays level, as if the island did not hear what the room heard.
Exclusive rider survived cross-examination. My face did not.
They filed the weekend as debrief and salt air. Almost-touch inventory: noted, denied, noted again.
Procedural night. I can survive procedural.
Pack at five. If you post *is this a date* with my badge in frame, I will revoke your witness clause.
The ferry horn answers like a stamp. Case two closes. Case three waits behind glass doors and an HR inbox.

She found the Office of Arts and Licensing again anyway, the deputy directors' wing where intake's mistakes came to be signed or denied. The plate still read Deputy Director. The hearing still glowed on his monitor, unmuted, as if the building had saved her seat.
Kitsu Kaoru let her in the way a gate let in weather: as fact, not favor. Cold mug. Files tied with string the stapler could not be trusted to hold.

The board member on screen clears his throat with performative patience. The chat lit up in order: *Unprofessional* from a ward tile. *Who is she* from someone who filed complaints for sport. *Hair like a press release* from a thread that used emoji in the official minutes.
Deputy Director, the board member said, your applicant is blocking the agenda.
My applicant is seated where I placed her. If the agenda cannot tolerate a witness, revise the agenda.
He mutes the gallery with two keystrokes, not apology, and types one line without looking at her: witness only, do not engage.

Tuesday in Ryoko Port opens the way audits open. Not with a knock, with a notification. Rain files itself against the licensing tower while a clip eleven seconds long teaches the whole channel a deputy director's voice.

Someone screen-recorded the Wrong Floor hearing weeks ago, back when it was only a routine Arts Council licensing stream nobody watched. *If the agenda cannot tolerate a witness, revise the agenda.* The internet revised nothing. It played the line forty thousand times, set it to a beat, and tagged the Council's account until the Council itself had to notice.
Deputy Director-sama, you are trending. Your one good sentence has a hashtag and a remix.

Trending is not a docket. Sit where I can see you and the inbox. People and Conduct, the office the Council refers conflicts to, opened a file at eight this morning, before the coffee was enforceable.

On Toa's phone the clip loops in a feed that does not care about packets. A councilor freezes mid-objection. A white-haired applicant sits in the wrong chair. The comments sort themselves into the usual castes.
The top comment says *who is the dancer*. The second says *HR nightmare*. The third is a recipe ad. The internet has no witness posture.
And someone clipped the part where you muted the gallery. They captioned it *deputy protects mystery girl*. I am the mystery girl. I have a name and an expired packet.
You have a current packet now. That is the problem the clip just made expensive. I signed it. You depend on it. A camera turned both facts into a story we did not write.
He does not watch the clip. He watches the inbox count climb, the way a man watches a tide decide whether to take the lower dock.

The HR wing is all glass and acoustic panels, a fishbowl that lets the building watch you stay calm. A liaison named in the calendar only as *People & Conduct* slides two folders across the table with the patience of a fault line.
Folder one: signatory of record, Kitsu Kaoru. Folder two: sponsorship dependent applicant, Kakita Toa. The clip put both folders in the same frame. HR would like the frame explained.
I walked into the wrong conference room once. I have read the plate every day since. Does the file know I read the plate now?

The liaison says, in the level voice of someone reading policy aloud, that the concern is not the wrong door. The concern is a signatory whose name appears beside a dependent the public has decided to find interesting.
The concern is conflict of interest. Stated plainly: a deputy who signs for an applicant he is rumored to favor. Rumor is not a finding. But rumor schedules meetings, and we are in one.
So the building thinks the rider says romance, and the rider says *not romance on letterhead*. We agree with the letterhead. The internet did not read the letterhead.
Before the liaison files, we decide the public posture. Choose, applicant. The clip is loud. Our answer should be quieter, but it still has to be an answer.
We post one statement. Plain. *The deputy seated a confused applicant and corrected a packet error. There is no story. There is a queue.* I will sign my own name to it.
Owning the narrative is a real strategy. It is also a microphone. If you take the microphone, you do not improvise. Dates and names only, even in a caption.
Then I do nothing loud. I keep witness posture. The clip wants a reaction. I give it a closed mouth and a current packet.
Silence is also a filing. Harder to misquote, slower to clear. You will sit in the comments for a week and not answer them. Some applicants cannot. Can you?
Back in the licensing wing, the sponsorship packet lies open under the desk lamp. His chop in the signatory box. Her name in the dependent box. Two boxes a camera turned into a couple.

Signatory of record means I answer for your compliance. Sponsorship dependent means your right to work in this port routes through my signature. That is leverage. I do not enjoy being someone's leverage, including my own.
You sound like a man reading his own name as a liability. I have practiced that face in studio mirrors. It is not a flattering port de bras.
He almost answers that. He files the almost where he files everything he intends to keep.
By noon her statement is live under her own handle, three sentences, no emoji, a queue number where a heart might go. The remix accounts hate that it is boring. Boring is enforceable.
I owned it. *Confused applicant, corrected packet, no story.* My follower count went up. My panic went down. Roughly even trade.
By noon she has posted nothing. The clip keeps looping without her. The silence reads, to everyone but her, like composure. To her it reads like sitting in the wrong chair and not getting up.
I stayed quiet. Witness posture. It turns out the hardest deliverable is the one where I do not defend myself out loud.
Either way the public narrative now exists in parallel with my actual calendar. Those two ledgers do not match, and HR audits the gap, not the gossip.

He turns his monitor toward her. The public narrative: a deputy and his favorite. The deputy's real calendar: thirty-one applicants, four inspections, a ferry receipt from a harbor weekend filed under *audit retreat*, and one row left blank on purpose.
The harbor weekend is in the calendar as audit. The internet would call it something else. Both readings are on the same row. That row is what HR will ask me to explain.
So the question is not whether we did anything against the rules. The question is which version of us goes in the permanent file. The clip's version, or the calendar's.
Correct. And the applicant gets a vote, because the applicant is the one the file outlives. Choose how we resolve the signatory conflict before the liaison chooses a template for us.
Recuse the signatory. Move my packet to a deputy with no hashtag. Clean conflict, clean file. You stop being my leverage. I stop being your liability.
Procedural and correct. It also means another desk reviews you, and I lose the only honest reason to keep you in my afternoons. I will file it anyway, if that is the version you can live in.

Or we tell the truth on a form. *Signatory and applicant have a personal relationship. Signatory discloses. Applicant consents to oversight.* Not romance on letterhead. Romance disclosed in the margin, where HR can read it.
Disclosure is the riskier filing. It survives the clip by agreeing with it, on our terms. You understand that once I write it, the port owns the sentence too, not just the harbor.

After hours the HR fishbowl goes dark and his office keeps one lamp. The couch remembers them. A blanket, a bowl of clementines someone keeps restocking and denying. Rain reads the window like a slow auditor.
I filed the recusal. Deputy Saito reviews your packet now. He is competent and he does not know your coffee order. That is the price of a clean conflict.
So you are not my signatory anymore. You are just the man who taught me witness posture and keeps clementines he claims he does not eat.
I wrote the disclosure in my own hand. *Personal relationship. Disclosed. Oversight accepted.* The port owns that sentence now. So, apparently, do I.
You put us on a form and signed it. That is the most romantic thing a deputy director can do. It is also, technically, paperwork. I am crying about paperwork.
The harbor weekend sits between them unspoken, the after-hours audit neither of them will caption. Her neck remembers a count. His calendar remembers a blank row he left on purpose.
If the clip ever finds the ferry receipt, I will deny everything in dates and names only. Saturday. Harbor. Audit. No poetry.
Whatever the harbor weekend was, they filed it as debrief and salt air. The clip never reached the ferry receipt. Some rows stay blank because someone chose to leave them blank.
The clip got the conference room and none of the quiet parts. I find I do not want the internet auditing the quiet parts.
The quiet parts are not on any portal. Blanket is still a loan against your noise. Clementine is domestic filing. Almost-smile inventory: pending, denied, pending again.
You almost smiled when I said I cried about paperwork. I have witnesses. The witness is me. I am very reliable.
Motion denied, To-chan. Effective in three business days, like everything I intend to keep. Go home before the building decides we are a story it can stamp.

She peels a clementine she did not ask permission to take, and the rain keeps its own minutes against the glass. The clip will loop until the channel finds a louder one. The file will close quieter than it opened.
...You are not wrong about the clerks. Note it, and say nothing. A read you cannot hold quietly will cost you more than a wobbled bow.
We held the line together. That is new, and I find I do not hate it. Do not let it go to your head before the stitches are even in.
Witness note: foreman detained, ledger seized, and my witness turned the cut that should have killed her. Write that line first. We will argue about the rest behind my screen, not on a wet dock.
Say his name aloud and you accuse a peer of the bench with a dead clerk and a petal-count. The Crane envoy writes that home, and this city eats the witness long before it eats the magistrate.

Now you understand the work. We do not close the big file. We keep it open on purpose, one witness chain at a time, until the day the record can hold his name without burning the clerk who wrote it. That is what a left hand is for.
I keep what signs willingly. You did not. Holding what will not stay is the one crime this office cannot file. Take your road, Kakita Toa. Walk it on your own paper.
The envoy exhales once, not a blessing, only a tally of who gains. The rival magistrate's colors leave before the wax cools.
The first week as his sworn left hand is not a triumph procession. It is runners, copied seals, and a quarter walk where the okami nod at her sash instead of her obi.
She passes him a segment anyway. He takes it without looking, as if hunger were a secret he refused to file, and her fingers on the peel a form he meant to seal later.
The scroll stays open a breath, then he rolls it closed himself. Quarter clerks on the left wall stop pretending they are not listening. No one reaches for chains. This is a parting, not a sentence.
The Crane envoy's crest finally rises. Whatever he writes home tonight, it will not be a scandal. It will be a dancer who kept her own name in a city that collects them.

The footsteps stop. Fabric whispers in the dark. A quilt lands on her side of the screen, heavy wool, unmistakably his, smelling of cedar, ink, and the sleep he will never admit to losing. Paper keeps rustling on his side anyway, as if some sealed bundle on the outer desk were already listening.

When it ends she does not perform purity. She crawls back to her futon with his blanket over her shoulders and something private cooling between her thighs, a sealed bundle of letters glaring from the outer desk like a runner who already knows too much.
Matter: administrative. No body. No numbered case file after closure.
Witness B ████████ (runner, age twelve): delivered three summonses across the Hour of the Tiger, each a few breaths apart. Subject signed without looking up.
First bell of the Tiger. Summons packet, third copy, wax still warm from the night clerk. Magistrate wing, inner screen, do not knock like a petitioner who wants theater.
Second bell of the Tiger. Second packet. Same crack. Same eyes on the line. Same stamp like a heartbeat the boy learns to fear and need.

A third bell, late in the Hour of the Tiger. Third packet. The boy's knees hurt. Through the gap he sees the magistrate pour a cup of water and leave it untouched beside three tea cups that were never his.
His grip does not loosen. Grey eyes on hers, too honest, and this time he does not reach for a witness-note to hide behind.
She has argued with him all evening. So she crosses the distance herself, on her terms and not his, and lets the choosing be the answer.

He does not sign the permit. But a provisional gate-chit slides across the lacquer, forward-dated, the ink barely dry: enough to keep the gate guards from hauling her in before she finds a better argument.
For one breath the magistrate is gone, and something almost like a smile sits where the ledger usually does, the kind he will deny by morning.

She gathers the travel kosode she packed that morning, the one that turned out to be true after all. The corridor she had learned by heart goes quiet behind her. He does not follow. He never once raises his voice, and that is the gentlest cruelty the city ever taught him.

She served the season and kept her own road. Somewhere a peer magistrate's wax stays warm and uncut, and Ryoko Owari goes on lying as politely as ever. Some files the city never closes. That, too, is an ending.
You seal your own renewals after the clerks go home, Magistrate. A man who trusted his office would be asleep by now.

Then he died here, in this room, behind a seal that was never yours, and the tide carried him down to the noble canal where the watch would write drowning. The slime on his sleeve ran the wrong way for a man who fell in downstream. He came from up here, in the licensed quarter, where the water still tastes of the Scorpion piers.
The clerk's second ledger is the thread. Night counts in one hand, day counts in the other, both his. He will trade the Chrysanthemum's name before he lets his own hang for the bolt room.

Magistrate-sama, the colors in the back row. He has not taken a seat, because to sit is to be entered in the record. Sixteen petals locked Jiro's room, cut by a hand that knew the Emerald office from the inside. A magistrate has been keeping the Chrysanthemum's wax warm this whole season.
So the root keeps growing, because the one hand that could cut it sits where no one dares write his name. That is your whole season, Magistrate. Five files, none of them ever truly closed.
You are letting me go. After all of it, you are simply... letting me go.

Months after People and Conduct closed the file, the harbor turned cold and the clip stopped being about her. Ryoko Port moves on the way a feed moves on. It finds a louder fool and forgets the quiet one.

Deputy Director-sama. You have been replaced. The channel found a louder clip. A councilor narrated nine minutes of a budget meeting with his microphone muted. The internet calls it *muted councilor energy*.
I am no longer the mystery girl. I am, at most, a footnote with good hair.
Footnotes outlive headlines. That is the only fame worth filing.

The crane on her tracksuit catches the lamp, gold over her heart, the same black jacket she wore into the wrong conference room a year of queue ago. She owns newer ones. She keeps wearing this one. It stopped apologizing in the shoulders somewhere around the harbor.

The People and Conduct fishbowl went quiet months back. The folder with two names in it closed, one way or another, on terms the building agreed to carry. The building wanted a story it could stamp. It never got one.
The disclosure sits in the permanent file in my own hand. *Personal relationship, disclosed, oversight accepted.* The internet, bored of the truth, went hunting for a man with a muted mic instead.
We kept it procedural. Another desk reviews your packet now, and the file closed clean. The internet, bored of clean, went hunting for a man with a muted mic instead.

He turns his monitor toward her, the way he once turned it to show her the gap between two ledgers. The calendar again. Thirty-one applicants, four inspections, a standing Friday row that used to read *audit retreat* in the dry font the portal assigns to everything.

It does not read *audit retreat* anymore. Someone has written over the row by hand. His hand. The row says, in ink, on a calendar the whole licensing wing can open, a date. Not the noun of it. The plain fact of it.
You filed a date on letterhead. In your own handwriting. You. The man who spent three cases insisting it was not romance on letterhead.
It was not, then. It is, now. I amended the filing. The letterhead caught up to the calendar. The calendar caught up to the harbor.
Effective when?
Effective immediately. No waiting period. I have run out of business days I am willing to make you wait.
Then I accept the filing as written. Effective immediately, no waiting period. For the record, I have wanted it effective immediately since the wrong conference room. I just never filed it.
Noted. Entered. The record agrees with you, which it rarely does and never out loud.

Objection, Deputy Director-sama. For three cases you told me everything you intended to keep was effective in three business days. I want my waiting period back. I have grown attached to the suspense.
Overruled. The waiting period was always for the building, not for you. I am done making you wait for the benefit of an audience that muted its own microphone.

That was when it happened, the thing he had denied for three cases, the motion he had ruled against every time she filed it. The corner of his mouth went, and kept going, and did not stop at almost. It landed.
A whole one, small and grey-eyed and without precedent in any file she had ever read. She did not breathe.
You smiled. I have witnesses. The witness is me. I am extremely reliable. It has been classified.
Noted.
He did not file it away. He did not say *motion denied*. He let it sit on his face where the building could have seen it if the building had cared to look.
Motion granted, To-chan. On the record.
Granted with no waiting period, after I argued for the suspense. I withdraw my objection. Slowly. Under protest. For the record.
Your protest is noted and overruled. I am keeping the smile and closing the clause.
Granted and effective immediately. I accepted the filing and the filing accepted me back. That is not how paperwork usually works.
It is how this one works. I wrote it that way.

They keep the harbor Airbnb now. Not as a clerical error. A line item with both their names on the booking and a lockbox that has finally learned the two of them. Rain comes back the way it always comes back to Ryoko Port, quietly and in quantity, and files itself against the cedar-framed glass.
You restock the clementines. You have always restocked the clementines. You denied it for a year.
Domestic filing.

Which was not a denial, which from him was a confession with the serial numbers left on. The blanket on the harbor sofa is no longer a loan against her noise. It is hers, or theirs, the distinction having quietly collapsed.
She sits in witness posture out of habit, hands folded, spine honest. He notices, because he notices everything.
You can sit however you want. You are not a witness here. You are the filing.
I like the posture. It is how I sit when I am paying attention. I am paying attention, Deputy Director-sama.
Then pay attention to this part. It is the part I did not put on any portal.
Then I will sit like a woman who stopped reading the plate to confirm she is allowed in the room.
She uncurls, slow, into something with no apology in it at all. He watches her do it the way he watches a tide decide whether to take the lower dock.
He takes the clementine peel out of her fingers and sets it on the armrest, bright and forgotten, the way it had been forgotten on a narrower couch in a glass building once.
Acceptable noise is still noise. The harbor has ears. The neighbors have a lease. We decide how loud the audit gets tonight, and you decide first.
We audited the rider once before, on the island, after hours. My neck still remembers the count. I came back for the rest of it.
We kept the island procedural. I have wondered, on every ferry since, what the unprocedural version files like.
Then choose, on the record. A quiet audit after dark, on your word, or we close the file here, warm and dressed, and let the rain keep its own minutes.
Audit it. Quietly. On my word, in dates and names only. You taught me the difference.
Close it here. Warm. Dressed. Your arm, the blanket, the rain. That is the whole filing tonight.
He draws the zip of her tracksuit down, slow, the way he does everything he intends to keep, knuckles tracing the bare line of her sternum where the gold crane sits warm over her heart.
Deliverable one. You beg the only way I allow after dark. Dates and names. Nothing performed for an audience.
Friday. Harbor. Kaoru. Please.

He counts under his breath, one, two, three, unhurried, refusing her the performance of shame and refusing, also, to stop, until her heel presses a careful bruise into his shoulder and the rain loses track of itself against the glass.
You do not perform gratitude on the furniture. You never did. You file it in the break room. I have the precedent in my own hand.
Already filed, Deputy Director-sama. The standing Friday, made flesh. Effective immediately.

After, he steadies her with his palm at her hip, the same bracket from a service elevator and a western inn and a couch the city used to own, and pulls her into the curve of his body so she can feel that the audit is, technically, never complete.

He pulls the blanket up over them both in the same patient order he does everything, and she fits herself into the curve of him while the rain keeps its own minutes on the glass. No audit tonight. Just the bracket of his arm, the one from a service elevator and a western inn and a couch the city used to own.
Acceptable noise is still noise. Tonight the acceptable noise is the rain and you breathing under my arm. The file can stay open until morning.
I can survive an open file. I have survived worse paperwork. This is the first one I do not want closed.
Three business days used to be how long I had to wait for everything you intended to keep.
You do not wait anymore. That clause is closed. You are not a deliverable with an effective date. You are a standing item.

She had argued for the waiting period out of habit and lost on purpose. The suspense had only ever been the building's. He had stopped scheduling her like a deliverable somewhere around the harbor, and she had let him.

She had accepted effective immediately the way she accepted most true things, late out loud and early in private. He had stopped scheduling her like a deliverable somewhere around the harbor, and she had let him.

On the calendar back at the tower he has left exactly one row blank, the way he used to leave one blank on purpose. A man should keep one row for the thing he has not scheduled yet. The next case. The next door. The next *unless*. He has stopped leaving the rest of them blank.
I still sit in witness posture sometimes. Old habit. It is how I sit when I am paying attention, and I am still paying attention. I read the plate before I open the door. I have for a long time now.
I stopped sitting in witness posture. I sit like the filing now. I still read the plate before I open the door, out of love instead of procedure. I have for a long time now.
She had been reading the plate before she opened the door for a long time now, and she no longer pretended she had wandered in by mistake. She had not. Not once since the first.
I file that under *kept*. In a place no portal can index. And I let the harbor keep its own minutes against the glass.
Disclosed. Oversight accepted. Effective immediately.

The fast track your letter promised is not a faster queue. It is a signature. A Council sponsorship is only valid once a deputy director signs for the applicant. I am the deputy director on this floor. That is the line your transfer letter left out.
So the fast track is a person. And I opened his door by accident, on camera.

If I sign your sponsorship, I swear to the Council that you are an artist and not a story about fraud waiting to happen. The board takes my word because I do not give it cheaply. So give me an artist to swear to.
And here I thought I was auditioning for a permit. I am auditioning for your signature.
I understand paperwork. I am very good at paperwork when someone explains the boxes. *Direct deputy review.* I read that line three times, and my pulse did something unprofessional each time.

Favoritism insurance. I document your inspections so the Council can see you are not handing permits to artists you happen to like. The irony writes itself. I am simply not allowed to laugh about it on the record.
Everything you offer is a calendar invite. The inspection, the weekend, possibly the rest of my life. I am starting to suspect the calendar is how you say the things you will not put in a sentence.
Witness posture, even here. I document the want and I do not perform it where a listing photo could see. My clause never asked me not to want him. It only forbade me to put it on letterhead.

Dependent. Signatory. Two boxes on one form, and a camera that turned them into a couple. I did not understand that my right to dance in this port was also your liability until you said it out loud on a balcony.

And if the Council decides the leverage looks like a favor, they can suspend the sponsorship, or revoke it, or hand my file to a deputy who never met me. My whole right to dance in this port is one sentence you signed. I keep forgetting that until a fishbowl reminds me.

A standing item. The Council files those the way it files rent and rain, the recurring things it expects to keep paying attention to. I have been a great many classifications in this building. That is the first one I would frame.
Three business days after the wrong conference room, Ryoko Port still files rain against every window it owns.
Kakita Toa's sponsorship packet now carries a deputy director's chop and a witness clause she did not read until it became mandatory.
It sounds like you attend, you document, and you do not perform gratitude on municipal letterhead. Again.
